Course Description: Pit crits are the core of the program in painting/printmaking. The beginning of each weekly session is an all-community meeting with students, the DGS, graduate coordinator, and those faculty members attending the crit. Two-hour critiques follow in the Pit; the fall term is devoted to developing the work of second-year students and the spring term to first-year students. A core group of faculty members as well as a rotation of visiting critics are present to encourage but not dominate the conversation: the most lively and productive critiques happen when students engage fully with each other. Be prepared to listen and contribute. Note: Pit crits are for current Yale students, staff, and invited faculty and guests only; no outside guests or audio/video recording are permitted.

The course supports the Painting/Printmaking Thesis exhibition through development of programmatic and publication-based elements that extend the show to audiences beyond Yale, as well as attending to the logistics of the gallery presentation. Studio visits initiate conversations about the installation of physical work in addition to considering the documentation/recording possibilities that allow the work to interface with dynamic platforms online and in print. The course introduces technology and media resources at CCAM and the Institute for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage at West Campus in addition to biweekly studio visits and group planning meetings. Editorial support is provided in order to enfold students’ writings and research with documents of time-based or site-specific work in an innovative and collectively designed publication. Enrollment limited to second-year students in painting/printmaking.

Course Description: What happens when, as visual artists, we narrow the gap between observing a subject and describing it? “Working from observation” is a phrase commonly used in art education, particularly in painting and drawing, yet is largely unexamined due to its rudimentary status in art school, associations with amateurism, and preliminary application in art practices throughout history. This seminar invites us to consider anew the creative and intellectual possibilities of observation through contemporary concerns, such as attention, reality, environment, objectivity/subjectivity, time, witness, and perception. Class periods and assignments will include a combination of hands-on learning, lectures, discussion, reading, and writing. Students will be invited to respond to experiential prompts in the media of their own choosing. Expert visitors in fields beyond and within the visual arts will deepen our understanding of how the body relates to the phenomenal and physical world. Readings and discussions will connect our discoveries to existing scholarship and research.

This course will survey the curatorial and scholarly work of renowned curator and thinker, Okwui Enwezor (1963—2019). Having curated some of the most important exhibitions in the last four decades, including the Johannesburg Biennial, the Venice Biennale, Archive Fever, and Documenta, to name a few, Enwezor's work has provided a much-needed framework for decentering conventional and Eurocentric canons that have continued to benefit the few (at the expense of others). Situated in what he once called a “change-agenda,” Enwezor's editorial, theoretical, and curatorial work engages with the core principles of representation and how these intersect with the construction and dissemination of culture. As he put it, “representation becomes not merely the name for a manner of practice, but, quite literally, the name for a political awareness of identity within the field of representation. In the context of decolonized representation, innovation is about the coming to being of new relations to cultures and histories, to rationalizations and transformations, to transculturation and assimilation, and new practices and processes, as well as the ways in which artists are seen to be bound to their national and cultural traditions.”  The seminar will engage such questions as: what can an exhibition as a vessel be? What is the lexicon of untranslatables that shapes a multipolar world? How can curatorial practice attune to the “lower frequencies” of unseen, opaque, and fugitive worlds-in-common? Amidst necropolitical catastrophe, what wagers of the in-common are we nonetheless able to stake?
Course Title: Curating the Global Contemporary: Enwezor and Legacies

Course Description: A hands-on, materials-based course, Fabric Lab explores fiber-related praxis through a series of investigations into weave structures, stitching, needlecraft, and knots, as well as the application and removal of color from fabric via printing and dyeing techniques. Instruction is intended to serve individual studio practice. Weekly meetings in the classroom space provide an opportunity to develop and share technical skills as a group in relationship to specific prompts. Readings and presentations contextualize our material explorations within contemporary art practice, unpacking historical hierarchies of “fine art” vs. “craft” and attending to the diverse social histories that underlie our engagement with textiles. The course includes some site visits, including an artist’s studio, a textile conservator’s workshop, and an institutional fibers department.
The course supports the Sculpture Thesis projects.

Limited to M.F.A. sculpture students. Critique of sculpture, time-based media, and ungainly projects. Students present their work in several venues in the sculpture building. Throughout the year a full ensemble of the sculpture faculty and students meet weekly for critiques in which each student’s work is reviewed at least once per term. During the spring term the format slightly changes to include evaluating work-in-progress, especially the thesis work of second-year students.
Limited to M.F.A. sculpture students. Criticism of individual projects.

For students entering the three-year program. This preliminary-year studio offers an intensive course of study in the fundamentals of graphic design and visual communication. Emphasis is on developing a strong formal foundation and conceptual skills. Broad issues such as typography, color, composition, letterforms, interactive and motion graphics skills, and production technology are addressed through studio assignments.
Limited to M.F.A. preliminary-year graphic design students.

For students entering the two-year program. The first-year core studio is composed of a number of intense workshops taught by resident and visiting faculty. These core workshops grow from a common foundation, each assignment asking the student to reconsider text, space, or object. We encourage the search for connections and relationships between the projects. Rather than seeing courses as being discreet, our faculty teaching other term-long classes expect to be shown work done in the core studio. Over the course of the term, the resident core studio faculty help students identify nascent interests and possible thesis areas.

This semester-long course supports first-year MFA graphic design students in developing an interconnected relationship between writing, research and practice. Through a combination of independent inquiry, writing prompts, group exercises, readings, guest lectures, workshops and acts of distribution, ‘Writing as Visual Practice’ approaches writing as a fundamental part of a practice. The course offers a space to actively consider the form of writing and to interrogate its role within a wider design practice, oscillating between the interiority of one’s own work or position, and the exteriority of external audiences and sources. In doing so, the course seeks to set the groundwork for independent thesis writing that follows in the second year of the program, and for an ongoing interrogation of broader modes and possibilities of writing, publishing, editorial and design practices at large.

For second-year graduate students. This studio focuses simultaneously on the study of established design structures and personal interpretation of those structures. The program includes an advanced core class and seminar in the fall; independent project development, presentation, and individual meetings with advisers and editors who support the ongoing independent project research throughout the year. Other master classes, workshops, tutorials, and lectures augment studio work. The focus of the second year is the development of independent projects, and a significant proportion of the work is self-motivated and self-directed.
Limited to M.F.A. graphic design students.

Like other art forms, typeface design responds to aesthetic ideas and currents, as well as functional, technological, and linguistic contexts and constraints. What does it mean to define a useful, original design brief for a typeface, and how can typefaces — understood as systems of recombinable letterforms and spaces — respond to design intent while honoring their intended functionality? This course explores articulating and evaluating design concepts for original type; researching, and working with, potential reference material; and bringing design ideas to life across a consistent and convincing set of original letterforms, while evaluating the work according to its intended usage. Aimed at intermediate typeface designers with some experience drawing and spacing type, the course focuses on building a consistent typeface design that responds to an original brief defined in consultation with the instructor. The course is taught using RoboFont, but is open to existing users of other font editors.

This course invites an in-depth examination of the digital tools that are integral to the graphic design practice. It is common for designers to default to industry-standard software, which can inadvertently narrow creative exploration. Our goal is to go beyond the usual limits by finding new ways to use current technologies, linking different tools together, and maybe even creating our own custom digital tools. We examine the technologies we currently use and search for new, maybe even unconventional, methodologies for creation and knowledge production. The course is structured around a series of lectures, group discussions, and hands-on workshops and culminates in a substantive project. This course does not require a background in software development, merely a willingness to engage with new media in novel and inventive ways. The workshops in this course cover a range of tools and techniques, including p5.js, Processing, Drawbot, InDesign Scripting, Web Scraping, OpenCV, and natural language processing. These sessions are designed to provide hands-on experience and enhance students' digital toolkit.

This course is a material interrogation of how to use, adapt and create structural supports for display. Over the course of the semester we will experiment with a range of methods and materials that situate graphic design within physical contexts. We will study models found in our daily lives, through exhibition visits, from visiting lectures. Students are expected to bring their own references for discussion and inspiration, each generating a sourcebook for ideas and techniques over the course of the semester. Together we will share ideas and resources, building towards collaboration when applicable. 

The coursework requires students to experiment with and apply the scaffolding methods using their own work and design practice. The semester is broken into three units of focus - each four classes in total. Each unit will include: examining models (either on site, with guest visitors, or in slides), & material experimentations in class, to culminate in final presentations and group critique. Students will work alone or in teams to problem solve material solutions for each thematic framework.
Open to second-year M.F.A. Photography students only. This class surveys the landscape of the contemporary photobook with a focus on producing a class book.

This required course supports the M.F.A. Photography thesis exhibition through attending to the logistics of the gallery exhibition as well as the development of programmatic elements that extend the show to audiences beyond Yale. Studio visits initiate conversations about the installation of physical work in addition to considering the documentation possibilities that allow the work to reach a wider audience, including editing and completing the portfolio and artist statement for its permanent home in Special Collections. The course introduces practical and conceptual considerations for exhibiting one’s work publicly and includes professional development resources and presentations for a life after Yale that sustains a lens-based practice, including an artist statement writing workshop, as well as group planning meetings and meetings with curators, gallery and museum professionals from Yale and further afield. Enrollment limited to second-year students in photography.

Each week, a guest artist working in a variety of disciplines addresses the cohort in whatever format they prefer—a round table discussion, conversation, or presentation— sharing experiences, insights, practice, and personal trajectory. The schedule of guest lecturers is student curated.
Course Title: This Means Something: Picture Makers Discuss Their Work and Practice

Course Description: Each week, four students present work for open review by a rotating faculty panel of artists, curators, and critics. Work can be presented as photographic prints, installation, video, performance, or in any other interpretation. Each student has two slots per term in addition to a final review twice a year.
Faculty 1: Gregory Crewdson, John Pilson, Elle Pérez

Course Description: Photographers continue to find themselves navigating the multiplicity of “contexts” their medium inhabits. This course examines various historical and contemporary examples of photographic “call and response” wherein artists find their way within both the obstacles and the opportunities presented to them by clients, curators, and editors, and (as students and teachers) within various pedagogical models. Through lectures, individual case studies, and student presentations we look to examples of authorship, artistic integrity, self-reflectivity, the exceeding of expectations, and convention-defying subversions that might just as readily be deployed within the context of a fashion spread as a museum, biennale, or government commission for an original work.
Course Title: The Assignment: Photography, Context, and Response from Classrooms to Commissions

Course Description: How do you build a system in real time? How do you design a technical assembly, an automation relay, a machine? This course will challenge students to develop complex systems using design tools that provide responsive feedback during the development process. Over the semester, each student will create a series of iterative prototypes, each exploring a key aspect of a larger project. Students will engage with both analog and digital circuits, sensor-driven networks, and mechanical systems, gaining hands-on experience with the material processes involved. Digital twins and simulations will be explored alongside physical models. Supplemental readings and discussion will review the evolution of prototyping in 20th and 21st century art and design. This course is offered in collaboration with the Center for Engineering Innovation and Design (CEID).

This course explores the artist’s critical relationship to the environment as mediated by “agential realism” – a framework developed by Karen Barad within physics, a field defined by questioning, experimentation, and conjecture. Due to our inability to visualize four spacetime dimensions (three space and one time), how does physics lend to building an artist’s language when matter and light effectively cease to exist? How does this exploration of nature and reality lend to extending the dimensions for production. By positing the artist’s inquiry within a quantum paradigm, and alternatively, the broader purview of the artist’s perspective into another field of inquiry, the course proposes a “laboratory” format of co-existence wherein research becomes, as the Belgian philosopher Isabelle Stengers writes in Another Science is Possible, “particularly insensitive to the questions posed by reality—not, by casting aside science’s actual claims, rather to retract from binaries of rational/irrational to allow for a generative conversation.” For example, how do the study of neutrinos and microbes become entangled with codes of justice, or with speculative imaginings beyond the human. This, to explore the potential in transdisciplinary elaborations on how nature really behaves, in the Kantian sense, as a reflection beyond the limits of reason. By referencing fiction, poetry, art practice and theory, and through immersive laboratory practices in visitations to the Yale Wright Laboratory, this course, developed in conversation with Molly Watts, graduate research fellow in Yale’s Department of Physics, refers to quantum physics as a way to confront the renewed conditions for the possibility of objectivity, the nature of measurement, the nature of nature and meaning, and the relationship between discursive practices and the material world. In addressing the quantum realm of interconnectedness as interpreted by physicists like Niels Bohr and Karen Barad – the entanglement underlying sociocultural phenomena is explored – between matter and meaning, material reality and discourse, to reassess the physical and metaphysical notions that rely on restrictive ideas about the physical world. The course will reference historical and contemporary artworks and art practices in conversation with science – for example, Hilma af Klimt’s early 20th c. work in the relation to the scientific developments in her time around hydrodynamics, machines, physics and astronomy, the mid 21st century critical practices of Robert Smithson, whose interest in the Second Law of Thermodynamics led to an interest to represent an “architecture of entropy” within the dialectical constellation of the site/non-site, and the contemporary practices of Tauba Auerbach who is compelled by the exponential notation in a geometric context. Readings will include Octavia Butler’s Parable of the Sower (1993), as a novel that unfolds as a mirror of the geometric properties of a parabola, the arch shaped curve codified by mathematical language as multiple, overlapping, and intersecting triangles to express the movement of time as a slippage between past, present, future.
Course Title: Quantum Studio: Differences, Contingencies, & Entanglements that Matter

Course Description: The four departments in the School of Art have critique opportunities for members of their individual areas. In the past faculty members have offered regular extra-curricular interdepartmental critiques on Sunday nights and Wednesday mornings. This course furthers that tradition by critiquing and discussing work by students from each department by those who are not familiar with the concerns, language, or material methods of a medium-specific field. By critique and analysis of each participant’s work, we attempt to break down the boundaries of medium and area. The course is designed for those who are interested in pushing medium orthodoxy aside to clear a space where and the development of language and renewed understandings are possible. Enrolled students exchange studio/desk visits with their classmates outside of class time as well as write about each other’s work. Each week, one shorter critique is offered by lottery to an M.F.A. student at the School of Art not enrolled in the class. This course is co-taught by multiple faculty and visiting critics, with one lead faculty member. Enrollment is limited. Permission of the instructor required.

A continuation of REL 3603. An introduction to the language of the Hebrew Scriptures: Biblical Hebrew. Students work through the grammar book, doing exercises and practicing paradigms. Among these exercises is the reading of specific biblical texts. By the end of the year, students should have a basic grasp of this ancient language’s grammar and some experience reading Hebrew.

Second term of a two-term introduction to the ancient Greek language of the New Testament for those with little or no knowledge of ancient Greek. The second term focuses on improving reading and translation skills and on developing working knowledge of the critical scholarly tools used in reading ancient Greek texts.

For centuries, Christians knew the Bible through the lens of its Latin translation, commonly known as the Latin Vulgate. This course is designed to introduce students to this version of the Bible, the most widely disseminated and read text from Late Antiquity to the early modern period. This translation of the Bible, composed primarily by St. Jerome and completed in 393, remained in broad use until the twentieth century and is still accorded a place of honor by the Catholic Church today. In this class, students eager to discover the medieval Bible for themselves are introduced to the Latin of the Vulgate Bible through some of its most famous passages. This introduction provides a basis for subsequent study of medieval, ecclesiastical literature and even ancient or early modern works in Latin. Along the way, we explore a variety of topics related to the history and culture in which the medieval Bible was used. Such topics may include, for example, Jerome and biblical translation, biblical interpretation, commentaries and the glossa ordinaria, the history of the book and paleography (ideally, with a visit to the Beinecke), and more.

The Emmaus narrative found in the gospel Luke encourages the reader to journey, to ask: what things? As faith leaders, we must consistently engage the critical issues, moments, and needs of our times, discerning what things matter most in our world(s). Together with partners in Puerto Rico, students from Andover Newton Seminary’s diploma program engage in meaningful dialogue, theological reflection, and embodied learning to best discern what that future can be. In so doing, students have the opportunity to learn constructively the art of building community within and among groups.

Reading courses may be arranged on materials, subjects, and concerns not included in the courses being offered, or may have a narrower focus than those courses. Reading courses may count toward distributional requirements across areas of the curriculum but may not be counted as fulfilling particular requirements within an area. Only full-time faculty at Yale University may offer reading courses.

The second of three small-group seminars required of M.Div. students. This course aims to enable students better to integrate the various aspects of M.Div. learning. This includes making academic connections between courses and areas of study; reflecting on the goals and process of theological education; attending to practices of spiritual formation; and considering how YDS coursework and activities may bear on students’ vocations. The course promotes peer learning, drawing on the experiences and diverse histories of cohort members as source material for overcoming divides between theory and practice and making connections between bodies of knowledge. In this second semester, a key theme is reading practice, in light of the core New Testament and History courses. We look at practices of scriptural reading, immersive and oral reading, and varieties of responses to reading, personal and corporate.

The Lutheran colloquium is offered each fall and spring terms. This year we explore the Lutheran Church in the public arena, capitalizing on resource people and the ELCA Social Statements. The colloquium gatherings are alongside student retreats, spiritual wayfinding, and weekly prayer. The primary focus is on students considering ordination in the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America, but it is open to all.

This one-hour weekly colloquium for ministerial formation, running over both fall (REL 3797) and spring (REL 3798) terms, deals with mentoring, theological reflection, and free church ecclesiology. Required of all M.Div. students enrolled in the Andover Newton program at Yale.
Course Title: Andover Newton Colloquium II: Ministry in the Making

Course Description: A thesis or project is an option in the third year of the M.Div. program. Theses or projects written for the M.Div. program are eligible for elective credit only.

A project or thesis is an option for both the concentrated and comprehensive M.A.R. programs. Students may elect to write a thesis in the second year of their program. Candidates who choose to write theses or pursue projects enroll for one or two terms, three credit hours per term.  For M.A.R. concentrated program students, the academic adviser determines area credit. Theses or projects written for the M.A.R. comprehensive program are eligible for elective credit only.

This is a practical course in worship and music, focusing on our situation in real time. Students are required to engage both in theological reflection and praxis of liturgy design and leadership. This is accomplished through reading, singing, active participation in class discussions, attending/experiencing worship, hands-on liturgy planning and leading, and evaluation of best practices. Creativity features prominently in the course through the student’s presentations.
Course Title: Andover Newton Colloquium IV: Designing and Leading Worship in a Time of Crisis

Course Description: Clinical Pastoral Education immerses ministry students in settings where they practice pastoral care under peer and professional supervision. Students who think deeply about what they need to learn in CPE, and how they might open themselves up to self-reflection, have more meaningful and effective CPE ministries. This 1.5-credit seminar prepares students for the intense internal and external work of CPE. This seminar meets once a week for six weeks of the spring semester.

“Mentoring” and “discernment” are two dimensions of ministerial formation that are nearly universally understood to be important. This colloquium provides students with a setting for intentional work in both areas. That setting serves as a holding environment for integration, where students consider how their YDS and Andover Newton educations are shaping their identities and visions for their futures. Cotaught with Andover Newton’s Associate Dean for Community Development and Student Formation Rev. JaQuan Beachem.
Course Title: Andover Newton Colloquium V: Mentored Vocational Discernment

Course Description: The Institute of Sacred Music Colloquium is central to the purpose of the Institute and to the faculty’s involvement in, and personal attention to, how ISM students are trained. Colloquium is the meeting ground for all Institute students and faculty, the place where we study together, grapple with major issues, and share our work as students of sacred music, worship, and the arts. Colloquium meets every Wednesday from 3:30 until 5 p.m., with informal discussion from 5 to 5:30 p.m. ISM students from the two partner schools of Music and Divinity collaborate on a presentation to be given in their final year. Students receive a letter grade for the term in which they present; all other terms are taken credit/no credit. The course is divided into two term-long parts, with responsibility for the fall term resting primarily with the faculty and outside presenters, and for the spring term primarily with the students.

Course Description: An extended paper, an independent thesis, or a project in the candidate’s area of concentration is required for the S.T.M. degree. Extended papers are written in conjunction with the regular requirements for courses credited toward the S.T.M. degree. Candidates who choose to write theses or pursue projects enroll for one or two terms, three credit hours per term.

This course explores the nature of biblical prophetic literature through a close reading of the book of Amos in Hebrew. Topics to be discussed include: the historical contextualization and referentiality of the prophetic message; the diachronic development of the prophetic text; the relationship between prophetic literature and the real-world institution of prophecy; the use of allusion, citation, and reference in prophetic texts; the theme of social justice; the form and function of poetry for conveying the prophetic message; and more.

A practical and theoretical introduction to the textual criticism of the Hebrew Bible and other ancient Jewish texts. We gain familiarity with the tools scholars use to compare and evaluate variants and variance in these texts. We also engage with the history of textual criticism as a discipline and with recent debates over its nature and goals. How might scholars chart textual development without enshrining problematic assumptions about the “original” text? How does textual criticism work in situations of major variance, when the absence of a defined boundary between composition and transmission is especially clear? What are the implications of complex and nonlinear transmission histories for modern textual tools like editions and translations?
Course Title: Hebrew Bible Textual Criticism and its Critics

Course Description: The Acts of the Apostles (Acts) is unique in the New Testament as the only sequel to a prior narrative (the Gospel of Luke). This course explores the literary, historical, and theological dimensions of the narrative(s) of Acts itself, paying additional attention to the many ways that this New Testament narrative has been interpreted in Christian communities over the centuries. Close readings and exegetical discussions of the text focuses on translation issues (no knowledge of Greek is expected, though students with Greek are encouraged to use it) and the author’s rhetorical style and art of composition, situating this story in its social and historical contexts and exploring the implications of various readerly perspectives (ancient and modern). Area I.
Course Title: Narratives of the Earliest Christians: Exegesis of the Acts of the Apostles

Course Description: The aim of this course is to introduce students to the religious landscape of Judaism in the Hellenistic and Roman periods, the landscape that provides the context for the emergence of the early Jesus movement. Emphasis is on appreciating the diversity of Jewish thought and culture in this time period and exploring how this diversity might influence our historical understanding of emergent Christianity. Area I.

​The texts of the New or Christian Testament emerged in the diverse social and complex political context of the Roman Empire and of second-temple Judaism. This course sets New Testament texts within their first- and second-century contexts, pays special attention to archaeological materials which aid our understanding of the world from which these texts emerged, considers how and why these particular texts came to be a canon, and pays special attention to themes of race, ethnicity, women, gender, imperial power and resistance to it, and varieties of Judaism in antiquity. Students also consider the vibrant and controversial contemporary contexts in which they and others interpret the New Testament, with particular focus on feminist, Black, and queer interpretation.

This seminar is divided into two parts. The first considers possible concepts of race and/or ethnicity in the ancient Mediterranean world, while the second focuses on racial/ethnic theory and minoritized hermeneutics. Ancient primary sources, the New Testament, and contemporary scholarship form the reading materials. While not required, previous completion of REL 505 and REL 506 is recommended. Area I and Area V.

One of the two most prolific and important authors in Second Temple Judaism is Philo of Alexandria. This course is intended to introduce the life, writings, thought, and reception of this important Jewish writer who has been called “the Jewish Plato” and “the first theologian.” We explore the Alexandrian Jewish community—perhaps the largest Jewish community in the Roman world, the social world of Philo and his family, introduce his vast corpus, introduce Hellenistic philosophy, and consider how Philo became “a church father honoris causa.” The course requires reading through the corpus Philonicum in an English translation, reading one or two articles per week, active participation in class discussions, writing a ten-to-fifteen-page paper, and taking a final examination. There is an optional Greek reading component for those who have training in Greek.

Ernst Käsemann famously stated that “Apocalyptic…was the mother of all Christian theology.” While he was urging a return to the study of apocalypticism in the teachings and life of Jesus, this course takes seriously a broader read of this statement: apocalyptic and the Apocalypse of John, via their protean nature, birth theologies, movements, art, film, violence, and further visions. Students consider both ancient contexts of Revelation (literary, sociohistorical) and its influence since in movements, times of crisis, art, and activism. Area I.

The course focuses on the reading of Biblical Hebrew texts but also offers a review of the elementary grammar of Biblical Hebrew and the introduction of more complicated grammatical concerns, especially syntax. The course introduces the student to Biblical Hebrew poetic texts, including those of Psalms, Proverbs, and the prophetic books. Students learn vocabulary from a textbook and consult an intermediate grammar for the study of syntax. The majority of each class is spent reading aloud a small portion of text, translating it, and studying the most important forms it contains and the elements of its syntax. Area I.

This course examines topics in the grammatical and syntactical analysis of biblical Hebrew. It introduces students to the fine points of the Hebrew grammar and syntax so that students are capable of reading the biblical text fluently and carefully.

This course is devoted to translating and interpreting the Greek text of 1 Corinthians and focuses on its major themes, e.g., Christ as God’s Sophia, the cross, the resurrection of the body, eschatology, the community as a “body,” the “assembly,” ministry, diversity and oneness, love and other ethical motifs. Special attention is paid to the letter’s teaching on women and gender, sexuality, and slavery. The course employs a combination of historical-critical and ideological-critical methods of biblical study. Area I.

This course, intended primarily for M.A.R. Hebrew Bible students, provides an overview of the latest developments in the field of Hebrew Bible, and the critical tools to evaluate and engage with them, including learning how to respond responsibly to others’ ideas both orally and in writing. Each week students read all or part of a recent scholarly work in the field of Hebrew Bible (approximately 200 pages per week). The works to be read are chosen in consultation with the instructor over the course of the term, in line with the academic interests of students enrolled in the course. Students are asked to critically evaluate those works in class; prepare an oral response as if on a conference panel; and write book reviews. The course operates as a workshop, with all student contributions heard, read, and critiqued by their peers as well as by the instructor. Area I.

This course introduces students to the history, theology and liturgical practices of Reformed worship. Students gain familiarity with: the ethos and characteristics of Reformed worship; Reformed theologies of baptism and the Lord’s Supper; the historical development, ordering, and function of elements within the Lord’s Day service; weddings, funerals and other occasional services, and some of the contemporary debates regarding Reformed worship practice. This course has been especially designed for students who are in the Reformed Studies Certificate Program or who are considering ordination in one of the Reformed denominations (Presbyterian, DOC, UCC).

The late antique period (ca. third to seventh centuries CE) marks a crucial phase in the formation of Christian liturgy—one that may best be described as an era of “creative ritual experimentation.” This course investigates the development of Christian liturgical discourse and practice (e.g., Baptism, Eucharist, occasional prayers) through the lens of three distinct yet interconnected categories of social actors central to the late antique religious world: church fathers, holy men, and ritual scribes. Drawing on textual (e.g., homilies, hagiography, hymnography), material (e.g., amulets, relics, ritual handbooks), and visual sources (e.g., frescoes, liturgical architecture) from across late antique Christendom—particularly Egypt, Syria, and Byzantium—students explore how liturgical traditions were articulated, performed, and contested in both ecclesiastical and everyday religious settings (e.g., households, saints’ shrines, local feasts). Prior coursework in liturgical studies, such as Foundations of Christian Worship, is helpful but not required.
Course Title: The Making of Christian Liturgy in Late Antiquity

Course Description: Combining biblical reflection with theological investigation, this course examines the potentially innovative character of Christian communities (both ecclesial and extra-ecclesial), across their varying dimensions. What, for example, might push Christian communities to open their doors to all comers, to turn outward in service to nonmembers, to shun efforts to secure themselves through accumulation of their own resources, or to violate the wider society’s principles of social distinction or legal requirements within their own borders? Interpersonal, political, and economic aspects of Christian community are examined, along with questions of how external boundaries are to be drawn and internal organization established.
Course Title: Radical Community: Christian Perspectives on Life Together

Course Description: This course is a survey of Christian hymnody and psalmody, and other congregational music from the early Christian Church to the present. This course examines the incredible Hymnal Collection of over 16,000 items in the Beinecke Library at Yale which makes it second largest in the United States to the Library of Congress. Through lectures, conferences, DVDs, videos, audio presentations, and class discussions, students engage in the application of the historical and theological content of the course, identify over 100 hymn tunes, enabling, planning and selecting congregational song. Area II and Area V.

This course is an introduction to Christian moral norms, ideals, and practices, and to some classical and contemporary disputes over their substance and application. Drawing upon a variety of historical and contemporary sources, we ask what difference Christian commitments make for assessing the ends that human beings pursue, the actions we permit and prohibit, and the traits of character we praise, tolerate, and admonish. We consider the ways in which Christian moral thinking is shaped by the Hebrew Bible and New Testament before considering interlocking questions concerning the ethics of the use of force, the economy, property, prison abolition, immigration, families, disabilities, environmental justice, and food.

It is getting harder for us to pay attention. Much of the research into the contemporary “attention crisis” attributes the problem to technological factors such as smartphones and social media. But blaming a tool that aids in destruction, however dangerous that tool may be, can only offer us so much insight into the underlying causes of the appeal of and drive to the destructive behavior itself. We also need to ask: what expectations do we have when we turn to face the world and how do these expectations determine our sense of what is worthy of our attention? How do different accounts of what the world is, who God is, and who we are in relation, shape the ways we conceive of the nature and importance of attention? Engaging with historical and contemporary accounts, this course explores the relationship between our different ways of seeing the world, God, and humanity, on the one hand, and the ways we construe not just the problems of distraction, but the purpose and promise of attention itself.
Course Title: Theology and the Crisis of Attention

Course Description: This course explores the continued development of the Anglican way of being Christian in the twentieth and twenty-first centuries, giving particular attention to the continued evolution of the Episcopal Church and emergence of the Anglican Communion, as well as the controversies that face Anglicans in their postcolonial situation. It is a companion to REL 6662, making a two-term study of the historical evolution and theological traditions of the Anglican way of being Christian. The primary aim of the course is to analyze and make a constructive theological assessment of modern Anglican traditions and to explore these as a pastoral and spiritual resource for Christian life and ministry. We do this by engaging in the study of both well-known and lesser-studied texts and figures. In addition to lectures, each week we discuss the respective texts, interrogating them with respect to the distribution of power, questions arising from colonialism, and issues relevant to the formation of the global Anglican Communion. These questions guide us: What does it mean to be Christian in the Anglican Way, and how do we do Anglican theology? How do we approach the study of the Anglican story in light of the dialectic between the Catholic and contextual, secular and Church, universal and particular, the global and the local? To what extent is the Anglican Way an exercise in depolarization? Area II and Area III.
Course Title: The Anglican Way II: Continuing Depolarization

Course Description: This course engages students in recent conversations around the theology and practice of baptism and eucharist. Beginning with the 1982 World Council of Churches document Baptism, Eucharist, and Ministry, we read texts that have emerged from ecumenical sacramental dialogues in the past three decades and discuss major issues such as mutual recognition of baptism, patterns of Christian initiation, who may administer the sacraments, and open communion. Area II.
Course Title: Baptism and Eucharist in Ecumenical Dialogue

Course Description: This course explores memento mori practices in a variety of religious traditions in order to assess how the remembrance of death affects everyday life and the degree to which the diversity of these implications for everyday life is conditioned by religious context. Prior course work in theology or philosophy is recommended. Area II and Area V.
Course Title: Remember Your Death: Memento Mori Practices in Comparative Perspective

Course Description: This course offers an introduction to Roman Catholic liturgy, including its history, theology, and practices. Given that the Catholic tradition spans nearly 2,000 years, encompasses numerous rituals and devotions as well as complex theological developments, and is practiced around the globe in diverse cultural contexts, this course is necessarily selective in its approach. We therefore examine a number of key topics that illuminate the historical development and contemporary practice of Catholic worship. Twentieth-century developments, especially the liturgical movement, the reforms of the Second Vatican Council and their implementation, and the continuing debates surrounding these developments within contemporary Catholic liturgical life receive particular attention.

This course explores the history, theology, values, and practices of Unitarian Universalist (UU) polity and their implications for ministry and congregational life. Students develop a framework for engaging questions of governance, authority, accountability, leadership, and community across congregations and diverse sites of ministry.
Course Title: Ecclesiology, Ministry, and Polity: Unitarian Universalist

Course Description: This seminar focuses on eighteenth- to mid-twentieth-century US missions in the region of greater Syria (encompassing Lebanon, Syria, Palestine, and Israel today). Using published scholarship as well as archival materials (largely English-language) at Yale Divinity School and elsewhere, students learn about the intertwined history of missions and education-building in these regions, as well as about work to translate Scriptures into Arabic and to disseminate them in various forms. We are particularly attentive to the role of women and markers of gender, ethnicity, and race as we find these in the archives. Each student develops their own archival-based research project, with the goal of contributing new knowledge in a conference paper, article draft, or other presentation, based in largely unpublished diaries, letters, and manuscripts. Research can be conducted into English, French, or Arabic materials. Limited to twelve students.
Course Title: Missions, Education, and Scripture in the Middle East

Course Description: This course introduces students to the history of global mission, surveying the practice of mission from the first century through the present day. Students gain an appreciation for the broad range of perspectives that have shaped missionary activity from its earliest beginnings, engaging with key texts that trace recurring themes across the patristic era, the Middle Ages, the Reformation, and the modern period. The course gives sustained attention to the complex and often contested relationship between mission and Western empire, inviting critical reflection on how power and culture have shaped—and reshaped—the missionary enterprise. Students also explore recent trajectories in mission thought, including indigenous agency, translation, and decolonial approaches, and consider their implications for the future of Christianity worldwide. Throughout, the course employs a World Christianity lens to evaluate the development and transformation of mission in the twentieth and twenty-first centuries.

This course examines the Reformation as the emergence of a radically new form of Christianity in the West, set within a period of profound social, political, and cultural transformation. It explores the dynamics of religious change by tracing shifting understandings of salvation and the Christian life, the relationship between church and society, the reconfiguration of ritual and the sacred, and the roles of violence and suffering in an age of upheaval. Particular attention is given to the problem of Protestantism itself: a movement that fragmented almost from its inception. By engaging its central, and often conflicting, convictions, the course asks whether Protestantism can be understood as a coherent religious project or whether it is better seen as a constellation of divided communities bound by shared tensions and debates.
Course Title: The Birth of Protestantism: The Reformation

Course Description: This graduate seminar investigates the transformation of magical practices and traditions amid the shifting political, linguistic, and religious landscapes of the ancient Mediterranean and West Asian world, with a special focus on the period of late antiquity (ca. 250–750 CE). The course approaches “magic” not as a timeless category but as a contested domain of religious discourse, both in antiquity and in modern scholarship. We consider how magic served as a potent site of interreligious contact and competition where specialists negotiated legitimacy and ritual efficacy was claimed and disputed. We attend to the ways that techniques, divine names, ritual substances, and cosmological assumptions moved across boundaries, whether through shared marketplaces of expertise or through polemic and prohibition. We trace trajectories of continuity and innovation across Mesopotamian, Egyptian, Israelite, Greek, Roman, Jewish, Christian, and Mandaean materials. Readings foreground primary sources in translation (e.g., ritual handbooks, amulets, and curse tablets), alongside critical scholarship in the history of religions, ritual theory, and material and textual cultures. By the end of the course, students are equipped to analyze “magic” as both practice and accusation, and to map late antiquity’s dense networks of ritual exchange, rivalry, and religious imagination.
Course Title: Magic at the Crossroads of Religious Traditions in Late Antiquity

Course Description: How do Christian discourses on and practices of confession, care, and conversion operate in modern productions of knowledge, dynamics of power, and modes of subjectivation? How does that religious legacy inform the political imagination of domination and resistance, recovery and revelry? This course approaches these questions by reading Michel Foucault’s own readings of religion in his later books and lectures in which he decisively turned to Greco-Roman antiquity and Christian patristics. It focuses on confession, care, and conversion as topoi in Foucault’s research and teaching from the first volume of his History of Sexuality (1976) to his last series of lectures on The Courage of Truth (1983–1984) shortly before his premature death from AIDS-related complications. In short, this course interrogates Foucault’s abiding interest in religion not only as a theorist of knowledge, power, and subjectivation but also as an activist with a Jesuit education attentive to queer styles of living.
Course Title: Confession, Care, Conversion: Reading Foucault Reading Religion

Course Description: From ancient journeys to the underworld to migrant deaths in the Mediterranean today, this course explores how people in Sicily have understood the passage between life and death. We bring poetry and philosophical reflection into conversation with funerary rituals, liturgy, tombs, sacred objects, and film, tracing how the island’s ancient cultures endure and change through centuries of migration and religious exchange. Christian burial rites, Jewish and Muslim practices, saints’ relics, and Palermo’s Capuchin Catacombs reveal how the dead remain part of everyday life, shaping religious devotion, artistic expression, and political struggles over land, borders, and memory. Combining literary analysis, historical inquiry, archaeology, liturgical studies, and ethnography with regular film screenings and close examination of material and visual evidence, the course invites students to explore death in Sicily through multiple methods and perspectives.
Course Title: Death in Sicily: Literature, Liturgy, Ritual, and Mortuary Politics

Course Description: This course surveys the history of Christian worship from its early Jewish and Mediterranean contexts through medieval Eastern and Western traditions, the Protestant and Catholic Reformations, and modern and global Christianity, including contemporary Protestant traditions. It explores how worship shapes Christian communities and how liturgical traditions acquire authority, sustain continuity, and undergo change. Close study of historical documents introduces the sources and methods of liturgical history, with particular attention to the relationship between prescribed rites and lived practice. Drawing on ritual and cultural studies, the course examines worship as embodied practice situated within particular social worlds, asking how it both reflects and shapes religious identities and relations of power. Lectures, discussion, student presentations, and three short papers develop the historical skills needed for further study of Christian worship.

Language about the senses and sense perception has often been used in descriptions of human encounters with the divine. From visionary experiences of God to discourse about how the senses aid in moral formation, many medieval and early modern thinkers believed that an experience with the divine was something that could be achieved in this life through the physical or spiritual senses. Some questions that are considered in this course are: What does it mean for someone to “see” or even “taste” and “touch” God? Is sensory language a metaphor or allegory, a description of transformed faculties, or an actual epistemological claim? How does the perception of God contribute to the knowledge of God? This course explores the way that medieval and early modern people described their experiences of sensing the divine. Tracing medieval and early modern discourses about sense perception during this period, this class offers different insights into the way Christians in these times periods people understood themselves, their worlds, and their relationships with God through the senses of sight, hearing, taste, touch, and smell. Area III.
Course Title: Sensing the Divine: Spiritual Senses and Sense Perception in the Medieval Era and Beyond

Course Description: This seminar traces the entangled histories of Sicily and Africa from antiquity to the present, when the island has become Europe’s southern frontier. Separated by less than a hundred miles of sea, Sicily and North African have been bound together for nearly three thousand years by conquest, commerce, enslavement, and migration. Carthage, the great city of ancient North Africa, governed western Sicily for more than two centuries; in the ninth and tenth centuries, Sicily was an Islamic province ruled from what is now Tunisia; in the twelfth century, Sicily’s Norman kings held the Tunisian coast; and by 1900 Italians in Tunisia, most of them Sicilian, outnumbered the French colonists. The course examines how this relationship was imagined, exploited, and remade in works of art, music, literature, and sacred practice. Particular attention is given to the rites, saints, and sounds that have crossed the channel in both directions, to the captivity and enslavement that underwrote much of what has been celebrated as Mediterranean convivencia, and to the historians, forgers, collectors, and curators who have written Sicily’s African past. By reading texts, images, objects, and music from each period alongside the scholarship that has interpreted them, the course examines both the entanglement itself and the ways it has been written and rewritten.

This interdisciplinary graduate seminar focuses on the display of religion in different global contexts and spaces, historically and in the present. “Display” refers to a multitude of ways in which religion comes into view materially, visually, and spatially: heritage sites, monuments, sculpture, painting, ritual decoration, processions and parades, memorials, and architecture, to name a few. What does it mean to “exhibit religion?” What are the rituals through which religion comes to acquire publicity or “publicness?” What are the sensory, affective, and material effects of the public displays of religion? Does the form of religious display impact its efficacy on viewers and practitioners from different faith communities? What does the politics of form—how religious display both attracts and offends sensibilities—say about social life, power, and hierarchy in different global contexts? How does religious display (of objects, bodies, material artifacts) intersect with the “everyday?” How might new theories of display enliven a “politics of aesthetics?” Course materials reflect the professors’ disciplinary and geographical expertise, spanning from South and Southeast Asia, Africa, to the United States (and various diasporas), with readings drawing from the fields of anthropology, art history, religious studies, and history, as well as a range of religious contexts. Other geographical/chronological interests and expertise are welcome and encouraged in student projects and class discussion.
Course Title: Religion on Display: Ritual, Publics, and Aesthetics

Course Description: The Middle Ages, defined by European culture as the period between 500 and 1500, is a period that witnesses the transformation of European Christianity into a Latin-speaking religious community under the Pope. It became increasingly separate from the developments in the Near East and Asia. For all too long this epoch has served in legitimating discourses of confessions, nations, and ethnic groups, such as in the nationalistic construction of the Germanic tribes. The course aims to draw a new image of these thousand years in terms of time, geography, ethnicity, gender, and culture. Medieval Christianity offers multiple possibilities for understanding both the perils and development of Christianity in an age of rapid change. On the one hand, the course examines processes of establishing power by exclusion, mainly of Jewish and Muslim believers, and of building strong hierarchies almost exclusively male. On the other hand, we find fascinating debates within Scholasticism about how to combine philosophical reason with Christian faith. Further, we explore the evolution of deep, inner spiritual practices among mystics, with special regard to female nuns, who were prolific writers. From this perspective we see how medieval Christianity is part of what we now experience as global Christianity, making a distinctive contribution to the emergence of a widely shared faith. Area III.
Course Title: History of Medieval Christianity: Learning, Faith, and Conflict

Course Description: This course offers a dynamic introduction to the history of Christianity by exploring some of its enduring myths. Each week, we investigate a different myth tied to the historical period under study, asking how these stories emerged and examining the ways they reveal or distort the truth. We consider the many questions our sources invite, recognizing both what they illuminate and what they conceal. Whose voices are we hearing—and whose are missing? Why have certain interpretations become dominant and enduring? What does that reveal about us? By engaging with these myths, we reflect on how to think historically and ethically about Christianity, considering contrasts between past and current perspectives, and how we might respond in our own time. Central to our work are the ways in which history continues to inform and challenge us today. Drawing on a rich range of primary texts, objects, visual materials, and secondary scholarship, the course invites students to explore the diversity of historical sources and interpretations—and to grapple with difficult and problematic questions.
Faculty 1: Teresa Morgan, Bruce Gordon, Tisa Wenger

Course Description: This lecture course, inspired by Howard Zinn’s classic A People’s History of the United States, foregrounds the religious experiences and voices of Black, Indigenous, Latino/a, queer, working class, and other peoples who have been historically marginalized in the United States and across North America. It asks how Americans have configured religion, especially Christianity, as an instrument of both oppression and resistance. Students learn how marginalized communities have reshaped Christianity and other religious traditions to sustain and empower themselves. The course introduces key debates in the religious history of North America and invites students to situate their own family stories in relation to the histories addressed in the course. Area III.
Course Title: A People’s History of American Religion

Course Description: This course, held at Beinecke Library, offers students an opportunity for intensive reading in and reflections upon the significance of early America’s premier philosophical theologian through a close engagement with Edwards’s manuscripts, published writings, and artifacts. Each session engages a selection of sources that highlights early modern social and material practices of intellectual production, Edwards’s particular practices, and the overlapping networks of relationships in which they were embedded. Area III.
Course Title: Jonathan Edwards’s Life and Thought as Seen in His Manuscripts

Course Description: In poetry, the lyric address refers to the “you” of a poem. Of course, in prayer, the “you” is most often either declared or assumed. How can we learn to write (and edit) prayers that serve purposes from private to public, using language in ways that is both pastoral as well as prophetic? Building on theopoetic analysis and readings of prayers and poetry, this class provides students with the capacity to write prayers in different registers, develop editorial skills, and both receive and give critical feedback. Some of the questions explored—in both readings and weekly assignments—are: what is the relationship of poetry to prayer? Does doctrine diminish the creativity of a poem? What role does form play in a prayer? Is community prayer a place for innovative theology, or should the emphasis be on communicating set ideas? How do concerns of justice, protest and assertion find place within a prayer? What does it mean to edit a prayer? This writing seminar is limited to twelve students. Roughly one third of the time is spent discussing assigned readings, with the rest of the time devoted to discussing contributions from the class. Admission to the class is on the basis of a paragraph detailing (1) interest in the class, (2) capacity to generate creative work, and (3) experience or willingness to respond fruitfully to critical engagement with the student’s contributions. Preference for second- and third-year students (but exceptions will be made for some first year students).

This course introduces students to public theology, public policy, and moral fusion movements in American history. Through a framework of moral analysis, moral articulation, moral agenda, and moral action, students are invited to examine how public theology has impacted the most significant advances in public policy in American history and why pastors and theologians of our time must practice in the tradition of moral leaders who have challenged systemic oppression in the public square and guided critical public policy shifts over the past two centuries. While it is commonplace in American public life to acknowledge that we are, as a people, “more divided than ever,” conversations about critical issues impacting our communities are consistently framed by a shared narrative of left versus right, liberal versus conservative, progressive versus traditional. This framing allows for a distorted moral narrative that focuses religious leadership and moral concerns either on a narrow set of personal issues or on wedge issues designed to perpetuate the left/right frame. Religion has been co-opted in American public life to serve the narrow interests of an extreme minority. Throughout this course, students are called to reimagine what public theology and moral action can look like today and how they can apply these historical lessons as they develop their own practice of theology. Area IV and Area V
Course Title: Introduction to Public Theology, Public Policy, and Moral Fusion Movements in America
Faculty 1: William Barber, Tony Tian-Ren Lin, Jonathan Wilson-Hartgrove

Course Description: 1 credit per term.

As individuals and communities engage religious diversity in ways they never have before, this seminar seeks to explore theoretical and practical issues in religious identity and interreligious community building. The course surveys stories and research on the development of religious identity, examines how interreligious relationships and communities are formed, and considers theological and practical rationales and methods. Within traditions, we explore problems of representation and diversity. Between religious traditions, we examine white Christian privilege in America and sources of religious discrimination and conflict. The class defines the qualities of effective interfaith relationships and identifies common mistakes leaders can make. Guest religious leaders from different religious traditions make presentations, students conduct interviews across traditions, and a final project seeks to create an interfaith community education experience. Area IV.
Course Title: My Neighbor’s Faith: Building Interreligious Community

Course Description: This course explores various approaches to college and university chaplaincy found in the United States in the twenty-first century. Drawing on a historical framework for the role of chaplaincy in the college setting from the middle of the twentieth century (when secularism became a heavier influence), and exploring the issues that enhance the vocation in a pluralistic context of the twenty-first century, the course provides an overview of strategies needed to offer a creative, current, and engaging chaplaincy in higher education. Through a series of lectures, open discussions, site visits, short chaplaincy narratives, guest speakers, and hands-on creative projects involving extensive group work, the class encounters numerous perspectives and approaches. The course is dedicated to the examination of individual points of view from college and university chaplains from various faith traditions and in different settings (i.e., small liberal arts schools, historically Black colleges, large research institutions, church-based schools) from across the country. These viewpoints also provide seeds for a deeper discussion of issues such as race, class, gender, and sexual orientation within college and university chaplaincies. Area IV and Area V.
Course Title: Models and Methods of College and University Chaplaincy

Course Description: This is the introductory course in theologies and practices of preaching. Students explore a rich variety of approaches to preaching, learn skills for exegeting listening communities, develop their understanding of preaching as public theology, and more. Attention is given to compelling biblical exposition, development of a powerful and supple homiletical imagination, reflection on the preacher’s spirituality, and ways to engage all of the preacher’s gifts for communication. The course includes plenary instruction and preaching sections in which students prepare and deliver sermons. This course meets the homiletics requirement for the M.Div. degree. Area IV.

This course addresses the theory and practice of faith-based conflict transformation in congregations and communities, in response to the growing prevalence of destructive conflict in faith communities and the wider society. Participants learn basic skills for leadership amid conflict, including understanding, engaging, analyzing and transforming conflict, as a critically important form of pastoral care. Using texts, case studies, role plays, and other resources, students compare and practice various models for addressing conflict in congregations; assess and work with students’ differing conflict styles and comfort levels to strengthen leadership in conflict situations; and consider various Christian theological understandings of conflict and its transformation. Area IV.
Course Title: Conflict Transformation: Pastoral Care with Congregations and Communities

Course Description: This course explores theories, perspectives, and approaches to educational ministry with youth. Students look closely at the context and world of youth and explore texts and media that take seriously the voices, dreams, questions, and struggles of adolescents. The class also looks closely at the role of religion and faith in the lives of adolescents—in particular, the role of Christian education and youth workers in the lives of young people. While acknowledging that there are myriad approaches to ministry and education with youth, in this course students wrestle with the question of what “must” be included, covered, or emphasized in good youth ministry. Area IV.

Divine action in the world is proclaimed in numerous ways: in music, visual art, literature, testimony, and performance, for example. When might such forms of expression constitute preaching? What are the boundaries of the sermon genre? How might preachers and other proclaimers learn from one another? The aim of this course is to explore the limits of the sermon genre and use the insights gained to enhance the preaching task. The assignments involve blurring the neat lines that separate preaching from other ways of bearing witness to one’s faith. The course examines the relationship between proclamation and identity, relying heavily on African American traditions of proclamation and resistance. Ultimately the course seeks to foster vibrant preaching and intellectual curiosity. Area IV.

When research focuses on a faith community or spiritual practice, unique questions emerge. There are practical, theological, ethical, and methodological considerations. How, for example, might faith leaders study communities that they also lead? How might power dynamics shape research in congregational contexts? What are the best strategies for studying a community’s spiritual practices and where are the pitfalls? This course explores practical theology research with attention to methodology, ethics, reflexivity, and analysis. These elements are explored through interviewing practitioners, examining research models, and the development of original research projects.

Does gender make a difference? What difference does attending to the lived experiences and perspectives of women make as we theorize about knowledge, education, religions, theology, and Christian practices? This course attempts to explore these questions through works that take seriously the voices and practices of women as they relate to knowledge construction, education, and faith development within religious communities, particularly Christian communities. The course has three interconnected foci: feminist, womanist, and postcolonial epistemologies; exemplars of women’s involvement in education as practices of freedom; and women’s development in religious communities. The first two areas attempt to broaden the conversation about what counts as knowledge (and who gets to decide) and to explore ways that women have participated in liberation struggles in academic and public arenas. In the last area, students explore some of the ways that women’s development has not been taken seriously in religious communities. In particular, this course explores examples of Christian theology and biblical interpretation that have at times thwarted the development of women and begins to open up approaches that empower women’s development. Area IV.

This seminar course introduces Roman Catholic spirituality and its practices, examining their historical development, theological foundations, and ritual expressions through the lens of the Second Vatican Council. In an era characterized by the “spiritual but not religious” trend, the course examines how the enduring traditions of Catholic spirituality offer a valuable framework for contemporary spiritual exploration. Students critically engage with both historical and modern texts to discover how these practices and values can enrich their own spiritual journeys. The course also examines the diverse expressions of Catholic spirituality, including various liturgical rites and the contributions of different lay movements and religious orders.

This course offers an interdisciplinary exploration of Christian spirituality, focusing on discernment and guiding students through its theological and practical dimensions. In a fragmented and polarized world, it encourages students to discern God’s call and respond meaningfully in their daily lives through lived theology. The course emphasizes both individual and communal spiritual formation and discernment. The first half examines classic figures and writings, including The Cloud of Unknowing, Catherine of Siena, Ignatius of Loyola, Teresa of Ávila, and Jonathan Edwards. This exploration enables students to draw insights from tradition and develop their personal and pastoral practices of discernment. The second half shifts to contemporary applications, highlighting modern voices such as Dietrich Bonhoeffer, David F. White, Henry Nouwen, and Elizabeth Liebert. We ground discernment in the practices of discipleship and dialogue, focusing on transformative spiritual exercises that underscore the connection between spiritual formation, social justice, and personal accountability.

This seminar is designed to allow students to pursue, in depth, themes raised in the introductory courses. The course’s overall consideration is how an educational leader trained at YDS can effectively “minister” to students, colleagues, and other members of school communities. Readings and discussions cover a range of topics including the tradition of faith-based education, school mission, pedagogy, worship, service programs, and ethical leadership in the “business” of schools (admissions, budgets, fundraising). The seminar also makes extensive use of case studies and simulations. For the major research project, each student pursues a topic of particular interest related to schools and educational leadership. Research includes direct experience, fieldwork/campus visits, and review of scholarship. Issues of race, class, gender, and sexuality arise in connection with topics considered in this seminar. Area IV and Area V.
Course Title: Advanced Topics in Educational Ministry in Schools and Colleges

Course Description: This course offers an in-depth study of narrative spiritual care, a poststructural practice that has roots in family systems and critical theory. Narrative care focuses on the importance of people’s stories, beliefs, and values, and the meaning-making process. Such care challenges destructive dominant narratives, such as racist, sexist, and/or homophobic narratives. It also identifies life-giving alternative stories—including biblical and theological stories—that help people re-author their lives. Narrative approaches to individual, couple, family, and collective (community) care are explored. Area IV.

Christian ritual is fundamentally situational: it is a lived, multisensory experience that cannot be fully comprehended when divorced from the physical spaces and material objects that facilitated it, and much of what is important about it cannot be understood outside the specific context in which it occurs. This seminar explores the dynamic intersection of liturgy, art, and architecture in Early Christianity and the Byzantine Empire. By moving beyond purely text-based theological studies, we examine how sacred spaces, monumental images, and liturgical objects actively shaped—and were shaped by—the rituals performed within and around them. While the majority of the class is devoted to the Divine Liturgy, its architectural accommodation, and the art associated with it, we also investigate other rites, like baptism, marriage, and processions. The goal is not to create a neat narrative matching art and ritual but rather to consider both as products of specific historical, social, and theological circumstances.
Course Title: Art and Ritual in Late Antiquity and Byzantium

Course Description: Hagiography, the writing of a biography or life of a saint, is one of the most prevalent genres of Byzantine literature. Hundreds of Lives survive, ranging in date of composition from the fourth to the fifteenth centuries CE. They are written in various style and language registers by authors of differing capacities, some of whom were eyewitnesses, while others lived decades or even centuries after the saint had died. The protagonists of these Lives were all sorts and kinds, and included people from diverse backgrounds, professions, social classes, and experiences. The study of hagiography (sometimes called “critical hagiography”) entails the scholarly engagement with such sources. While issues of authenticity and veracity dominated earlier scholarship, in recent years Byzantine Lives have been recognized as important sources for social, political, and religious history, for cult building, ideology, and propaganda, and windows to how Byzantines perceived and understood their world.

An investigation of ethical challenges posed by developments in artificial intelligence, with attention to how various philosophical positions and religious commitments might bear on these challenges. One significant focus is questions about whether machines could share in those features that give human beings their moral and spiritual significance. Could we build AIs that are capable of suffering or flourishing? Or that can appreciate beauty, exercise moral responsibility, or experience the divine? How should individuals and society navigate uncertainty and disagreement about the moral standing of AIs? Alongside these questions about the metaphysical and moral status of current and future AI systems, we will also consider how engagement with AI might affect human purpose and flourishing. Does intensive cognitive reliance on AI pose a threat to human autonomy and human excellence? How should we evaluate deployments of AI in religious contexts? What moral principles and values should guide AI behavior in a pluralistic society? Is the prospect of artificial “superintelligence” something we should welcome, or something that we should oppose?
Course Title: Artificial Intelligence, Philosophically and Theologically Considered

Course Description: This graduate seminar thinks with and beyond modern categories of music and religion in the study of twenty-first-century Korea. Recent articulations of disciplinary “turns” in music studies and religious studies—each toward the other—provoke a central question that grounds our course: What shifts in our understanding of Korean life occur when we refuse to relinquish the entanglement of religion and music in our interpretive praxis? Reading across ethnomusicology, religious studies, and anthropology, we first examine Korean religions—shamanism, Buddhism, Christianity—with one ear attentive to the undertow of music and sound. We then turn toward Korean music—especially jazz and K-pop—with the other ear attentive to the cantus firmus of religion. Finally, we zoom in and out of the center and fringes of Korean nationhood—gugak and unsounded musicalities—to contemplate how music and religion, reconstituted through their mutual entanglement, can shed light on contemporary Korean life in ways that propel forward our conversations in the humanistic study of the Pacific Basin.
Course Title: Music, Religion, and the Study of Korea

Course Description: This course is designed as an exploration of the discourses, practices, institutions, and structures that have shaped and continue to shape Judaism as a tradition and Jews as a social group. Its goal is to provide students substantive engagement with the Jewish tradition and with the Jewish historical experience. Like other “religious civilizations,” Judaism cannot be reduced to a clear, unchanging set of beliefs, practices, and values. What Judaism is or should be has always been a matter of contention, even as the answers have changed over time and across context. The course is thus organized around a series of questions or problems with which Jews—and the study of Judaism—have perennially wrestled. Area V.

This course examines W.E.B. Du Bois’s contributions to the study of religious, ethical, and political thought, especially on matters related to the enduring significance of chattel slavery and its afterlives, racialized capitalism and political economy, and black internationalist criticisms of American empire.
