Students develop sophisticated language skills through working with authentic written materials, images, and videos concerning historical events, historical figures, artists, writers, and philosophers. Activities include working with translation tools, discussions, debates, presentations, oral and written exercises on platforms such as Playposit and Perusall, and collaborative projects.
Course Title: Advanced Chinese through History and Art

Course Description: We read and discuss modern short stories, most written prior to 1949, for the purpose of developing advanced language skills in reading, speaking, and writing.

Advanced language course with a focus on speaking and writing in formal styles. Current affairs are used as a vehicle to help students learn advanced vocabulary, idiomatic expressions, complex sentence structures, news writing styles and formal stylistic register. Materials include texts and videos selected from news media worldwide to improve students’ language proficiency for sophisticated communications on a wide range of topics.

Advanced language course that familiarizes students with Chinese business terminology and discourse through discussion of China's economic and management reforms, marketing, economic laws, business culture and customs, and economic relations with other countries. Case studies from international enterprises that have successfully entered the Chinese market.

Continuation of CHNS 1700 with more intensive study of particles, complex sentence structures useful for both classical and modern Chinese texts, and the reading and interpretation of famous texts from the Chinese canon.

This course is designed to help advanced language students develop an independent reading practice in modern Chinese literature, building the skills to read fluently and with confidence. It bridges the gap between reading Chinese literature in a language class environment and engaging with it for academic inquiry and personal enjoyment. Students explore a range of fictional writing, spanning the 20th century to the present. Through guided close readings and translation exercises, they are encouraged to attend to questions of form and style, historical context, and author biographies. Such careful reading is combined with an introduction to some of the major themes and debates in Chinese literary studies, to be determined each year by the course’s instructor. As students develop their reading competencies, they thus also begin building the framework needed to think critically about a text and its position in literary history. Readings for this class are in Chinese, with discussions in English. L5 Chinese or equivalent.
Course Title: Guided Readings in Modern Chinese Literature

Course Description: How often do you think about the Roman Empire? And why do some people ruminate about it so much? This first-year seminar looks at Rome as a conceptual resource, explored across 5 thematic units: history and politics, film, literature, popular media, and material culture. Designed as an introduction to Rome and its reception, the course studies how Rome’s legacy was constructed, contested, and mobilized after antiquity. What are the uses of Rome after Rome? Which Rome are we talking about? And how does an ancient civilization inform modern culture? Participants will learn to critically engage with textual and visual material, improve written and oral communication, and use primary and secondary sources to make succinct, well-supported arguments.

This first-year seminar is about how the stories we tell shape us, our values, and the culture(s) we live in through the lens of Greek and Roman mythology. Land can be many things depending on our worldview: ancestor and relative, home, country vs. city, nature vs. cultivated place, unknown opportunity, resource, or property. Students in this class gain a deeper understanding of the land stories they inherit, what they wish to continue to carry forward, and what they may need to leave behind to live in accordance with their values. Together we think concretely about Greek and Roman myth and the resonances and dissonances with the wide range of land stories that shape our world. Key Course Questions include: 1a. How could these myths affect Greeks’ and Romans’ relationship to and with land? 1b. What are our relationships to land? 2a. What values are promoted in Greek and Roman myths about land? 2b. How do these stories reflect and enact cultural values? 3a. How is land characterized? 3b. Is land gendered? 4a. What is the role of violence in shaping these characters’ interactions with each other and with land? 4b. How is this violence framed in the narrative?
Course Title: Myth, Land, and Power: Reading Ancient Greece and Rome

Course Description: Ancient Athens was the birthplace of democracy — a radical experiment in popular rule that flourished, evolved, and collapsed within two centuries. But the democratic experiment never really ended. This course traces how the ancient Athenian democracy was built, how it functioned, its institutions, its leaders, its limitations, and its skeptics. We also attend to the afterlife of Athenian popular rule: the centuries of criticism, contestation, and reinvention through which the Athenian government became a (real or imaginary) template for many constitutions people live under today.
Course Title: The Origins, Criticisms, and Legacy of the Athenian Democracy

Course Description: Greek tragedy is both a literary and a theatrical phenomenon. It emerged in the ancient city-state of Athens and peaked in the 5th century BCE. The distinct rules governing its poetic composition and theatrical execution were repeatedly renegotiated across cultures in the modern era – including in Greece. The course investigates the inherent tension of Greek tragedy as both “poem” and “performance script” through a parallel study of its texts (in English translation) and filmed stagings from around the world. Students develop a clear understanding of the subject matter of Greek tragedy, alongside its historical, artistic, and socio-political contexts and conventions in antiquity and in modern times. Through systematic exposure to and rigorous analysis of textual, directorial, design, and performance choices, they explore the theatrical possibilities of Greek tragedy in modern times and cultivate their own directorial and dramaturgical thinking.

Modernity's fascination with the myth of Dionysus. Questions of agency, identity and community, and psychological integrity and the modern constitution of the self. Manifestations of Dionysus in literature, anthropology, and music; the Apollonian-Dionysiac dichotomy; twentieth-century variations of these themes in psychoanalysis, surrealism, and magical realism.

This course studies the political and cultural dynamics of free speech and freedom of expression in Greco-Roman antiquity in order to lend historical depth to, and invite the sampling of alternative perspectives on, similar issues in our own day. The main point of focus in the class is on humorous free speech as practiced in certain accepted and ‘rule bound’ forms, such as comedy, oratory, iambic invective and satire, and the breaking of the rules in those same forms, as well as in certain non-sanctioned kinds of aggressive expression such as graffiti, anonymous pamphlets, off-script improvisations in comedy and mime, and public shaming rituals. We look into the questions of who can get away with saying what in the ancient world, and how the parameters of acceptable humor and abuse were set and policed. Students examine the cultural politics that are built into the rules, as well as the particular habits of humorous expression, both proper and improper, as they came to be practiced in certain political milieu (Archaic Greece, Democratic Athens, Republican Rome, Rome under the emperors), by certain persons (slaves, freedmen, elites, males, females, foreigners, the young, and the old) in certain historical contexts (e.g. in the aftermath of triumphs and failures), for certain purposes (e.g. to celebrate, to resolve crises, to do political work, to censor and punish, and so on).
Course Title: Laughing Matters: Satire and the Limits of Free Speech in Ancient Greece and Rome

Course Description: The history and culture of the ancient world between the rise of Macedonian imperialism in the fourth century B.C.E. and the annexation of Egypt by Augustus in 30 B.C.E. Particular attention to Alexander, one of the most important figures in world history, and to the definition of "Hellenism."
Course Title: Alexander the Great and the Hellenistic World

Course Description: The origins of Greek philosophy lie in the period before Socrates and Plato. The so-called Presocratics set up many of the questions developed by Plato: the nature of being, the structure of matter, human knowledge and its limitations, causation, etc. Three of the most important early Greek thinkers are studied in this course: Heraclitus, Parmenides, and Empedocles. Knowledge of ancient Greek is not required.

This seminar examines the lives of women and enslaved people in the ancient Greek world, primarily in the fifth and fourth centuries BCE. We engage with ancient sources such as historical texts, dramas, legal speeches, inscriptions, art, and archaeological sources, as well as current scholarship, and attempt to confront the challenges and gaps in the ancient evidence on women and enslaved people, two groups whose experiences are often excluded, mentioned in passing, or caricatured, and whose voices are often absent in these sources. The course focuses on source work, interrogating the ancient evidence for information it might not be trying to tell us, and evaluating the use of different kinds of sources in communicating the lived experiences of women and enslaved people. Over the course of the semester we consider the following major themes: What questions can we ask about the lives of women and enslaved people? What sources and methods can we use to get at the answers to these questions? How do we write historical narratives about them, and examine the power structures entangled with their lives and the violence enacted against them?
Course Title: Women and Enslaved People in the Ancient Greek World

Course Description: For students who wish to pursue a specialized subject in classical civilization not otherwise covered in courses. Students are expected to provide a detailed reading list and a clear outline of their project early in the term. The work should result in a term paper or examination. A limited number of these courses may be offered toward the major.

Tutorial for seniors in Classical Civilization. As a culminating experience in the major, the student completes under the supervision of a faculty member an original research project, intensive language and literature study, or a creative endeavor. To register, the student must submit a written plan of study for approval by the director of undergraduate studies and the faculty instructor. Fulfills the senior requirement for the B.A. degree.

Tutorial for seniors in Classics. As a culminating experience in the major, the student completes under the supervision of a faculty member an original research project, intensive language and literature study, or a creative endeavor. To register, the student must submit a written plan of study for approval by the director of undergraduate studies and the faculty instructor. Fulfills the senior requirement for the B.A. degree.

For marginalized groups, histories of misrepresentation and misnaming significantly curb archival holdings' legibility, even when entries are searchable in public databases. What alternative online architectures can intervene here, enabling faithful (digital and in-person) identification and accessing of objects? What are our responsibilities to Indigenous peoples when we bolster European minority collections? And how might in-group knowledge and epistemes combine with scientific understandings, as well as anticolonial guidance from Indigenous Studies, Asian (American) Studies, Jewish Studies, and Latin American Studies, to shape just archival structures? This course leads students in critically evaluating the varied, often problematic representational choices of artists/authors with works placed throughout Yale collections. It does so via collaboration on a searchable collections guide for literary, artistic, and testimonial materials created by and/or about Romani peoples, who as Europe’s largest minority (and with a U.S. population of over one million) are amply present in university collections such as Yale’s but have little say over how objects depict, describe, or name them. As the course's structural practicum, this work integrates, into public-facing webpages, the learning that students undertake about relational minority representation on Indigenous lands and about Romani-related holdings in Yale's Beinecke Library, Art Gallery, Fortunoff Holocaust Testimonies archive, etc.
Course Title: Minority Archives on Indigenous Grounds: Yale's Romani Collections

Course Description: This course provides a hands-on, project-based introduction to a foundational period of early modernity in the West associated with the Renaissance. Focusing on five technologies that shaped the course of modern societies—the printing press, paper-making, spinning and textile production, medical innovation, and mapmaking—we read primary and secondary sources, visit Yale’s collections, and experiment with our own prototypes and models to understand the intellectual watershed of 1500-1700. We take an interdisciplinary and multimedia approach, grounded in literary texts, but with explorations into a wide range of fields to recreate the cultural tapestry of a period before our current disciplinary divisions came into being. Though anchored largely in European materials, the course adopts a global perspective as we investigate how the imperial and commercial expansions of these centuries shaped the networks, migrations, and flows that characterize the world today. Structured as a hybrid seminar-studio course, students should come prepared to both discuss, write, and make objects in class.

Where do the dry, who-what-which details set down on a census form meet the far messier and richer reality of the people whose names are scrawled there? And how might a writer bring that meeting about? What can a shoebox of doodle-filled letters tell us about the ways that friendship, art, war, sex, and politics struck a couple of New York novelists, c. 1941? How do we respond as writers and as a culture when faced with the lack of such inky particulars? Blending seminar and workshop, this class is meant for students who want to write literary non-fiction based on archival materials. In an intensive, hands-on fashion, we’ll dig into documents of all sorts as we read essays and excerpts from belletristic works that wrestle with the sometimes slippery fact of the archive. Throughout, we’ll ask how best to bring vital prose into being. Weekly writing experiments that draw from various Yale collections and beyond will encourage students to see and respond to archival discoveries freshly and for themselves. A semester-long writing project will take shape as an extension of that seeing and responding. While no previous archival experience is required, this class calls for a serious commitment to the written word. By permission of instructor. Limit 12.
Course Title: Writing from the Archive: Imagining the Real

Course Description: This course is required for students in the certificate on Collections: Objects, Research, Society. Students propose a capstone project with one of Yale’s cultural heritage institutions in conversation with the certificate directors. The project must involve practical experience in the field as well as a substantial reflection component. Possible projects include assisting with the curation of an exhibition, reparative archival description, ongoing bibliographic projects, provenance research, scientific conservation analysis, museum-related research and study, metadata development and analysis, collections-based research etc. The capstone culminates in either a final paper, a public presentation, or other project (in consultation with the certificate directors).

An undergraduate seminar on the life and work of one the greatest poets of all time, and founder of modernity, Charles Baudelaire (1821-1867). Readings include œuvre de jeunesse, his collection of poems in verse, Les fleurs du mal, his collection of poems in prose, Le spleen de Paris, as well as his writings on fashion, contemporary culture, drugs, the arts, especially painting, his translations from English and American including Edgar Allan Poe, his private journals, the infamous late writings on Belgium and the Belgians, as well as his rare attempts at theater. His afterlives in literature, painting, music, dance, film, translation, and philosophy. Secondary materials including but not limited to Benjamin, Bonnefoy, Derrida, Fondane, Sartre. Readings in French, discussions in English.

This course helps students build a toolkit of theories and approaches to literary comparison. We compare texts within genres, across genres and media, across periods, and between cultures and languages. We consider questions such as whether all comparisons must assume a common ground, and whether there is always an implicit politics to any comparison. Topics range from theories of translation and ekphrasis to exoticism and untranslatability. Readings include classics by critics such as Aristotle, Ibn Sina, and Kristeva, and writers such as Marie de France, Nezami, and Calvino. It also engages with the literature of our own moment: we read a newly-translated novel and a contemporary poet visits the class for a conversation. We also discuss films and a computer game.

Development of ways to engage films from around the globe productively. Close analysis of a dozen complex films, with historical contextualization of their production and cultural functions. Attention to the development of critical skills. Includes weekly screenings, each followed immediately by discussion.

The genre of tragedy from its origins in ancient Greece and Rome through the European Renaissance to the present day. Themes of justice, religion, free will, family, gender, race, and dramaturgy. Works might include Aristotle's Poetics or Homer's Iliad and plays by Aeschylus, Sophocles, Euripides, Seneca, Hrotsvitha, Shakespeare, Lope de Vega, Calderon, Racine, Büchner, Ibsen, Strindberg, Chekhov, Wedekind, Synge, Lorca, Brecht, Beckett, Soyinka, Tarell Alvin McCraney, and Lynn Nottage. Focus on textual analysis and on developing the craft of persuasive argument through writing. Formerly ENGL 129.
Course Title: Tragedy in the European Literary Tradition

Course Description: The genre of tragedy from its origins in ancient Greece and Rome through the European Renaissance to the present day. Themes of justice, religion, free will, family, gender, race, and dramaturgy. Works might include Aristotle's Poetics or Homer's Iliad and plays by Aeschylus, Sophocles, Euripides, Seneca, Hrotsvitha, Shakespeare, Lope de Vega, Calderon, Racine, Büchner, Ibsen, Strindberg, Chekhov, Wedekind, Synge, Lorca, Brecht, Beckett, Soyinka, Tarell Alvin McCraney, and Lynn Nottage. Focus on textual analysis and on developing the craft of persuasive argument through writing. Formerly ENGL 129.
Course Title: Tragedy in the European Literary Tradition

Course Description: Islamic civilization has produced numerous works that would make it onto almost anyone’s list of wondrous books. In this course, we read a selection of (or from) those books and study the literary and intellectual cultures that produced them in an attempt to deepen and nuance our understanding of Islamic civilization. Readings include the Qur’an, classical Arabic poetry, the Shahnameh,  Leyli ve Mejnun, the Conference of the Birds, the Hang Tuah Epic, and much else besides. All readings in translation.

Medieval understandings of womanhood examined through analysis of writings by and/or about women, from antiquity through the Middle Ages. Introduction to the premodern Western canon and assessment of the role that women played in its construction. This course counts as a LxC course.

A survey of major French novels, considering style and story, literary and intellectual movements, and historical contexts. Writers include Balzac, Flaubert, Proust, Camus, and Duras. Readings in translation. One section conducted in French.

This course introduces students to a diverse group of modern Jewish poets—from Gertrude Stein, Moyshe Leyb-Halpern, and Adrienne Rich to Muriel Rukeyser, Yehuda Amichai, Paul Celan, Edmond Jabès, Leonard Cohen, and others. Writing in English, Yiddish, German, Hebrew, and French, these poets gave seminal expression to Jewish life in a variety of modes and permutations, and in the process produced poems of lasting and universal value. The class explores work as art and considers pressing questions of cultural, historical, and political context. All readings are in English.

Modernity's fascination with the myth of Dionysus. Questions of agency, identity and community, and psychological integrity and the modern constitution of the self. Manifestations of Dionysus in literature, anthropology, and music; the Apollonian-Dionysiac dichotomy; twentieth-century variations of these themes in psychoanalysis, surrealism, and magical realism.
Close reading of major novels by two of Russia's greatest authors. Focus on the interrelations of theme, form, and literary-cultural context. Readings and discussion in English.

This course is an introduction to Japanese literature written in the last fifty years, with a focus on women writers. Since the 1970s, Japanese women writers have increasingly appeared on the shelves of international bookshops and on the lists of international prizes. These authors have experimented with multiple genres, from romance to horror, and depicted diverse worlds, from the daily grind of working women to the simple pleasures of eating and cooking. Over the course of a semester, students encounter a new novel each week that introduces them to the world of contemporary Japanese literature. Novels are selected around a different theme each year. This year, the focus will be on novels that address loss––losing loved ones, losing memories, losing minds, losing composure, losing a sense of reality––and recovery from that loss. Original-language versions of texts can be made available.
Course Title: Japanese Literature After 1970: The Art of Losing

Course Description: The 14th-century Persian poet known as Hafez is one of the most beloved, respected, and influential lyric poets in world history. His playful, provocative, sublime, ambiguous poems permanently transformed how people wrote about the pains of love, getting wasted at parties, and communing with God, not only in Persian-speaking Iran and Central Asia but across Eurasia, from the Balkans to India and from Siberia to Indonesia. When Westerners began reading his verse in the age of colonialism, his example inspired transformations in the literary theory, poetics, and philosophy of major figures such as Goethe, Sir William Jones, Byron, Hugo, and Nietzsche. This course considers the works and reception of Hafez from his own time and place through his many afterlives, down to the present-day uses of his poetry. As well as reading the Divan of Hafez, we encounter his works in the numerous ways he has been received down the centuries: we memorize and recite poems, listen to musical interpretations, practice traditional divination with his poems to answer questions about the future, and read a contemporary Uzbek novel about an A.I.-powered avatar of the poet.

An introduction to the first literary movement of Spanish American origin, Modernismo.  At the turn of the 19th century, breaking away from Spanish Peninsular influence, modernistas looked to other languages and cultures for inspiration: from France, the U.S. and the Far East to the rich legacy of indigenous myths and traditions. Fighting for their countries' national sovereignty and for modernization, they also explored class and sexual identities and opened the way for increased participation of Spanish American women authors in literature and culture. Readings of poetry, essay, and narrative from José Martí, Manuel Gutiérrez Nájera, Rubén Darío, Delmira Agustini, Juana de Ibarborou, Lola Rodríguez de Tió, Leopoldo Lugones, Julio Herrera y Reissig, and Amado Nervo, among others. Taught in Spanish.
Course Title: Critical Contexts in Latin America: Understanding Spanish American Modernismo

Course Description: Changing narratives, themes, styles, and aesthetic ideals in current Brazilian prose and poetry. The writers' attempts to express or define a personal, national, and global consciousness influenced by the return of political democracy to Brazil. Focus on readings published within the last five years.

An examination of the concepts and assumptions in contemporary views of literature, including theories of meaning, interpretation, and representation. A critical analysis of new criticism, formalism, psychoanalysis, reader response, structuralism, poststructuralism, new historicism, Marxism, and postcolonial, feminist, queer, and cultural studies approaches to literature.

This course combines a seminar on the history and theory of translation (Tuesdays) with a hands-on workshop (Thursdays). The readings lead us through a series of case studies comparing, on the one hand, multiple translations of given literary works and, on the other, classic statements about translation—by translators themselves and prominent theorists. We consider both poetry and prose from the Bible, selections from Chinese, Greek, and Latin verse, classical Arabic and Persian literature, prose by Cervantes, Borges, and others, and modern European poetry (including Pushkin, Baudelaire, and Rilke). Students are expected to prepare short class presentations, participate in a weekly workshop, try their hand at a series of translation exercises, and undertake an intensive, semester-long translation project. Proficiency in a foreign language is required. Previously ENGL 456.

The German Democratic Republic (1949-1989) was a political and aesthetic experiment that failed, buffeted by external pressures, and eroded by internal contradictions. For forty years, in fact, its most ambitious literary texts and films (some suppressed, others widely popular) explored such contradictions, often in a vigilant, Brechtian spirit of irony and dialectics. This course examines key texts both as aesthetic experiments and as critiques of the country’s emerging cultural institutions and state censorship, recurrent political debates and pressing social issues. Texts by Brecht, Uwe Johnson, Heiner Müller, Christa Wolf, Johannes Bobrowski, Franz Fühmann, Wolf Biermann, Thomas Brasch, Christoph Hein; films by Slatan Dudow, Kurt Maetzig, Konrad Wolf, Heiner Carow, Frank Beyer, Jürgen Böttcher, Volker Koepp.

We live in a world that is increasingly quantified and made subject to measurement across various dimensions. We have long been accustomed to think of the study of culture as primarily qualitiative, but the relatively new field of digital humanities tends to argue that present-day computational tools, up to and including those produced by the currently ongoing generative AI upheaval, have put at our disposal the capacity to supplement our traditional interpretive study of culture with digital methods that can enrich, augment and sometimes even question the insights we obtain from qualitiative inquiry alone. Looking at textuality as paradigmatic of the humanistic study of culture, with a combination of readings and hands-on tinkering, explore this approach and its limitations. Methods investigated in the course is a selection of modern twenty-first century computational techniques such as vector semantics, topic modeling, and commonly used frameworks and toolkits for machine learning with text. No prior computer programming knowledge will be assumed, and the course itself teaches students the extent of programming expertise needed in the Python programming language to put together customized text processing and analysis workflows from existing open-access building blocks and libraries.
Course Title: Culture as Data: Thinking Computationally with Text

Course Description: Introduction to the classical and modern theory of sovereignty in the context of G.R.R. Martin’s A Song of Ice and Fire (source material of the Game of Thrones TV series). Though Martin's novels are not a work of German literature, they now belong to the canon of world literature. They address theoretical, literary and historical discourses which became prominent in the German context, especially in the period 1871-1968. Students will learn to analytically bridge contemporary fiction, theory and history. Major themes of Martin's literary universe include: tragedy, agency, myth and religion, history and modernity, realism and romanticism, environmental catastrophe and geopolitics.
Course Title: Game of Thrones and the Theory of Sovereignty

Course Description: The Holocaust as it has been depicted in books and films, and as written and recorded by survivors in different languages including French and Italian. Questions of aesthetics and authority, language and its limits, ethical engagement, metaphors and memory, and narrative adequacy to record historical truth. Interactive discussions about films (Life Is Beautiful, Schindler's List, Shoah), novels, memoirs (Primo Levi, Charlotte Delbo, Art Spiegelman), commentaries, theoretical writings, and testimonies from Yale's Fortunoff Video Archive.

What can the Humanities tell us about climate change? The Humanities help us to better understand the relationship between everyday individual experience, and our rapidly changing natural world. To that end, students read literary, political, historical, and religious texts to better understand how individuals both depend on, and struggle against, the natural environment in order to survive.

Was Sappho a feminist? This course tries to answer that question by analyzing how women’s voices have been appropriated by the literary and cultural canon of the west–and how in turn women writers and readers have reappropriated those voices. Students read a generous amount of literary (and in some cases, musical) works, along with a variety of contemporary theoretical approaches so as to engage in conversation about authorship, classical reception, and materiality. Following an introduction to Greek and Roman texts key for problematic female figures such as sirens and sibyls, we turn to two later historical moments to explore how women artists have both broken out of and used the western canon, redefining genre, content, and style in literary creation writ large. How did Renaissance women such as Laura Cereta, Gaspara Stampa, and Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz fashion themselves as authors in light of the classical sources they had at hand? And once we arrive in the 20th and 21st centuries, how do Sibilla Aleramo, Elsa Morante, Anna Maria Ortese, and Elena Ferrante forge a new, feminist writing via classical, queer and/or animal viewpoints?
Course Title: Dangerous Women: Sirens, Sibyls, Poets and Singers from Sappho through Elena Ferrante

Course Description: This course offers a critical survey of Italian cinema from the postwar period to the present. It begins with neorealism, the movement that placed Italian cinema at the center of international film culture in the late 1940s, and moves through the modernist experimentation of Antonioni and Fellini, the popular genres of commedia all’italiana, the politically engaged cinema of the 1960s and 1970s, and the diverse, often memory-haunted cinema of today. Organized into five blocks (neorealism and the urgency of the real; the economic miracle and its discontents; modernism and the crisis of the subject; politics, body, and power; and contemporary Italian cinema), the course reads each film as an aesthetic object, through close attention to cinematography, editing, sound, performance, and narrative form, and as a historical document of a society in transformation. Students engage with debates on realism and representation, auteur theory, genre, and the relationship between cinema and political life, and apply these frameworks in discussion and writing. No prior knowledge of the Italian language or culture is required. All films are screened in Italian with English subtitles.
Course Title: Italian Film from Postwar to Postmodern

Focusing on five technologies that shaped the course of modern societies—the printing press, paper-making, spinning and textile production, medical innovation, and mapmaking—we read primary and secondary sources, visit Yale’s collections, and experiment with our own prototypes and models to understand the intellectual watershed of 1500-1700.
