Course Description: A broad introduction to the history of Jewish culture from the late Middle Ages until the present. Emphasis on the changing interaction of Jews with the larger society as well as the transformation of Judaism in its encounter with modernity.
Course Title: Modern Jewish Politics: The Last Four Centuries

Course Description: This course traces the development of animosity toward Jews and Judaism in different time periods and by diverse cultures, beginning in classical antiquity and continuing until the present. Through close examination of primary documents and the analysis of a variety of secondary sources, students build their understanding of the long history of this animosity, which we commonly refer to as “antisemitism.” There is also an ongoing discussion of the difficulty of assigning a simple definition to a phenomenon that has been referred to as “the longest hatred.”
Course Title: Introduction to the History of Antisemitism

Course Description: This class is an effort to reckon with the often-wrenching complexity of the Israel–Palestine conflict by focusing on films – documentaries, features, and hybrid works – that grapple in one way or another with its various human dimensions. We discuss these movies in relation to both their subject matter and the methods of their creation—the narrative, visual, verbal, psychological, and other choices made by the filmmakers. Our goal throughout the semester is to consider questions of politics and perspective, the role of imagination in documenting and enduring a sustained national struggle, the place where personal stories meet the larger sweep of history, and more. We focus primarily on films made over the last twenty years. We invite a few directors to participate via Zoom to discuss their work. There will be several out-of-class screenings.
Course Title: Watching Israel/Palestine: Emotions, Narratives, and Conflict on Film

Course Description: This seminar approaches the two most studied phases of Italian history, the Renaissance and the 20th century, by placing what we call 'otherness' at the center of the picture rather than at its supposed margins. The main aim is to challenge traditional accounts of Italian culture, and to look at pivotal events and phenomena (the rise of Humanism, the rise of fascism, courtly culture, the two World Wars, 16th century art, futurism) from the point of view of Black, Queer, and Jewish protagonists, authors, and fictional characters. Our theoretical bedrock is offered by modern and contemporary thinkers such as Fred Moten, Edouard Glissant, Eve Sedgwick, and Hannah Arendt. Our primary sources come from cultural epicenters of Renaissance, Baroque, and late Modern Italy, such as Leo X papal court, fascist Ferrara, 17th century Venice, and colonial Libya. In class, we adopt a trans-historical, intersectional, and interdisciplinary perspective inspired by current scholarship and early modern ideas of temporality, identity, and belonging. Themes and issues are analyzed at the crossing of the two historical phases and of the three topics in exam, and the material includes historical and theoretical analyses, narrative texts, poems, films, and visual art.

This seminar returns to one of history’s most consequential institutions – kingship – asking what millennia of Jewish engagement with royal power can teach us about sovereignty, representation, and dependency. Judaism’s relationship to kingship is profoundly ambivalent. The same tradition that produced enduring royal theologies also harbors a deep and systematic suspicion of monarchs. This tension is not a contradiction to be resolved but a generative force that has shaped Jewish political culture from antiquity to the present. The course traces this double stance from the Hebrew Bible through encounters with Near Eastern, Hellenistic, and Roman rulers; Jewish negotiations with Christian and Muslim medieval sovereigns; the age of absolutism; and the republican transformations of the nineteenth century. It concludes by examining how these dynamics persist in modernity through Zionism, the establishment of a Jewish state, and the reemergence of antisemitic tropes about Jewish power.
Course Title: King of the Jews: Royal Power and Jewish Political Culture, Ancient to Modern

Course Description: This class explores ancient models of Jewish textual production as contemporary conceptions of authorship and authority are shifting drastically. Pairing varied pre-modern models of Jewish text production and consumption with contemporary ruminations on our rapidly changing textual landscape, our course asks: is AI best conceived as a return to pseudepigraphy, wherein a text is attributed to a famous legendary author who didn’t write it? Or should we see AI as ancient authors viewed their literate slaves: as tools that privileged elites could use and never acknowledge? Conversely, AI can help us understand diverse modes of ancient text-production. Maybe late antique rabbis’ avoidance of single-author monographs in favor of collective anthologies is more legible amidst contemporary suspicion of books, essays, and poems that claim to be the work of a single human author but are demonstrably not so. This class further explores historical developments that explain the ultimate suppression of anything other than the single-author model. With these dynamics thrown in higher relief, perhaps we’ll be able to better understand why,  in 2026, we reflexively rely on such an impoverished vocabulary that often compels us to dichotomize a wide range of literary techniques as either “authentic” or “fraudulent
Course Title: Pious Forgery from Ancient Judaism to Artificial Intelligence

Course Description: This course looks at contemporary representations of social, political, and domestic space in Israel through cultural production such as literature, visual work, and art. It focuses on close reading of major Israeli works in translation with attention to how their themes and forms relate to the Israeli condition. Reading and viewing include: Amos Oz’s major novel A Tale of Love and Darkness, Anne Frank: The Graphic Diary, Maya Arad’s novella “The Hebrew Teacher,” TV show Arab Labor and writing by Yehudah Amichai, Etgar Keret, and Sayed Kashua, among others. We discuss topics and theories of personal and collective identity formation, war and peace, ethnicity and race, migration, nationalism, and gender. This course counts as a language across the curriculum (LxC).

This course examines the stereotyped, mythologized, and much-maligned figure of the Jew in visual culture throughout history, from the medieval period to the present day. How has this antisemitic archetype shaped the world we see around us, and how has it in turn been shaped by that same world? During the course, we will explore the shifting contributions of visual culture to the creation and dissemination of antisemitic tropes, including forms like cartography, architecture, political cartoons, theater, and film. The course will be primarily discussion-based and include significant in-class use of primary source material, as well as opportunities for students to critically investigate areas of personal interest.
Course Title: Antisemitic Visual Culture since the Middle Ages

Course Description: Jewish culture and society in Muslim lands from the time of the Prophet Muhammad to that of Suleiman the Magnificent. Topics include Islam and Judaism; Jerusalem as a holy site; rabbinic leadership and literature in Baghdad; Jewish courtiers, poets, and philosophers in Muslim Spain; and the Jews in the Ottoman Empire.
Course Title: Jews in Muslim Lands from the Seventh to the Sixteenth Centuries

Course Description: This seminar explores the history of right-wing political thought from the late eighteenth century to the present, with an emphasis on the role played by religious and pagan traditions. This course seeks to answer the question, what constitutes the right? What are the central philosophical, religious, and pagan, principles of those groups associated with this designation? How have the core ideas of the right changed over time? We do this by examining primary tracts written by theologians, political philosophers, and social theorists as well as secondary literature written by scholars interrogating movements associated with the right in America, Europe, Middle East and Asia. Though touching on specific national political parties, institutions, and think tanks, its focus is on mapping the intellectual overlap and differences between various right-wing ideologies. While the course is limited to the modern period, it adopts a global perspective to better understand the full scope of right-wing politics.
Course Title: The Global Right: From the French Revolution to the American Insurrection

Course Description: This course introduces students to the history of the term antisemitism as well as historical debates about its manifestations.  It focuses on Europe from the end of the nineteenth century, tracing the emergence of antisemitism in its modern form through interwar fascism and to the present, emphasizing discussions about whether a “new” antisemitism has emerged and focusing on efforts to restrain its manifestations by defining it broadly to include criticism of Israel.  We cover the central historical moments in the history of antisemitism in Europe, including the Dreyfus Affair, pogroms in the Pale of Settlement, Nazi Jew-hatred, and the twinning of antisemitism and anticommunism in the specter of the Jewish communist, dubbed “Judeo-Bolshevism.” The last few weeks of the course are devoted to the rise of Islamophobia in Europe and its relationship to antisemitism, as well as current discussions of antisemitism’s resurgence.
Course Title: Antisemitism in Modern European History since 1900

Course Description: Students study how Jews and Christians interacted on a daily basis as medieval Europe became more restrictive and antisemitic, a contributing factor to the Holocaust. In this writing seminar, students discuss a variety of primary sources in class–laws, stories, chronicles, images–while researching and writing their own seminar paper structured by sessions on topics, bibliographies, and outlines.
Course Title: How the West Became Antisemitic: Jews and the Formation of Europe 800-1500

Course Description: By the time Nazi Germany invaded the Soviet Union in June 1941, the USSR had become home to the world’s largest Jewish population—more than five million people. Roughly half would perish in the Holocaust. With Operation Barbarossa, the systematic mass murder of European Jews entered a new and decisive phase. Despite a substantial and growing body of scholarship, the Holocaust on the Eastern Front remains one of its less thoroughly explored dimensions. This seminar examines the Holocaust across the territories of the former Soviet Union, focusing on the distinctive forms it assumed in Ukraine, Belarus, Russia, Latvia, Lithuania, and Moldova. We study not only how Jews were murdered, but who they were, how they sought to survive, how they resisted, and how they fought Nazi Germany in the Red Army and partisan units. Particular attention is paid to local collaboration in identifying, robbing, guarding, deporting, and murdering Jews, as well as to postwar investigations and trials of collaborators. The seminar also explores Soviet and post-Soviet memory of the Holocaust and its place in contemporary debates over occupation, collaboration, national identity, and victimhood. Students engage with competing scholarly interpretations and work extensively with diverse primary sources.
Course Title: The Holocaust on the Eastern Front: History and Memory

Course Description: The Holocaust as it has been depicted in books and films, and as written and recorded by survivors in different languages including French and Italian. Questions of aesthetics and authority, language and its limits, ethical engagement, metaphors and memory, and narrative adequacy to record historical truth. Interactive discussions about films (Life Is Beautiful, Schindler's List, Shoah), novels, memoirs (Primo Levi, Charlotte Delbo, Art Spiegelman), commentaries, theoretical writings, and testimonies from Yale's Fortunoff Video Archive.

Writers of “historical fiction” have the advantage of knowing “how history turned out”—and it is one of the primary goals of this class to investigate how that knowingness has influenced their fiction. In this course, we will read nine novels from the genre, analyzing each for its relationship to the period of its setting (its approach to concepts of facticity and verisimilitude, both in the physical details and in the prose style) and to the period of its writing (an analysis as much political as literary), with the hopes of developing an understanding of how fiction “about the past” is often also fiction “about the present.

This course combines a seminar on the history and theory of translation (Tuesdays) with a hands-on workshop (Thursdays). The readings lead us through a series of case studies comparing, on the one hand, multiple translations of given literary works and, on the other, classic statements about translation—by translators themselves and prominent theorists. We consider both poetry and prose from the Bible, selections from Chinese, Greek, and Latin verse, classical Arabic and Persian literature, prose by Cervantes, Borges, and others, and modern European poetry (including Pushkin, Baudelaire, and Rilke). Students are expected to prepare short class presentations, participate in a weekly workshop, try their hand at a series of translation exercises, and undertake an intensive, semester-long translation project. Proficiency in a foreign language is required. Previously ENGL 456.

This course introduces students to a diverse group of modern Jewish poets—from Gertrude Stein, Moyshe Leyb-Halpern, and Adrienne Rich to Muriel Rukeyser, Yehuda Amichai, Paul Celan, Edmond Jabès, Leonard Cohen, and others. Writing in English, Yiddish, German, Hebrew, and French, these poets gave seminal expression to Jewish life in a variety of modes and permutations, and in the process produced poems of lasting and universal value. The class explores work as art and considers pressing questions of cultural, historical, and political context. All readings are in English.

This seminar introduces students to Jewish texts, histories, and book cultures through hands-on explorations of manuscripts, printed books, ephemera, and material objects in Yale’s extensive collections. Each week, students learn about a unique Jewish text or genre: Bibles, rabbinic literature, Passover haggadot, Esther scrolls, codes of Jewish law, custom books, communal records, liturgical and devotional works, newspapers, amulets and incantation bowls, oral testimonies, and personal archives. Correspondingly, in each session students also explore a different aspect of (Jewish) book history: the diverse formats and materials of texts (e.g., clay and wax tablets, scrolls and codices, papyrus, parchment, and paper); processes of production (e.g., manuscript making, printing techniques, book-binding), methods of illustration (e.g., illumination, woodcuts, engraving), modes of reading and studying, ritual and liturgy, censorship and circulation, and technologies of non-written texts, including audio and video recordings. Throughout, students encounter the global and multilingual history of Jews, Judaism, Jewish literatures and cultures from all over the world – Europe and North Africa, the Middle East and the Americas, East Asia and India – in languages such as Hebrew, Aramaic, Yiddish, Ladino, Judaeo-Arabic, Judaeo-Persian, Spanish, German, Italian, and English. The course also highlights connections, intersections, and disjunctures of Jewish, Christian, and Islamic (book) histories.
Course Title: Jewish Book History and Material Cultures: From Scrolls to Video Cassettes

The course focuses on reading, writing, speaking, and listening to Khmer words, long sentences, and texts. The course also emphasizes grammar, sentence structure and using words correctly.

The course learning activities include interactive, interpretive, and presentational communication; critical analysis; creative and authentic language applications in formal/informal contexts.

Course Description: This course teaches Hanja, the Chinese characters commonly used in modern Korean society. The main goal is for students to master 300 basic Hanja that frequently appear in Korean vocabulary. Through various materials, students explore how these characters are integrated into Korean words and how these words are used in everyday contexts. By engaging with these concepts, students enhance their understanding of Korean vocabulary and improve their overall proficiency in the language.

The history and organization of the Inca empire and its impact on the nations and cultures it conquered. The role of archaeology in understanding the transformation of Andean lifeways; the interplay between ethnohistoric and archaeological approaches to the subject.

Portuguese is a pluricentric language that is spoken not only in Brazil and Portugal, but also in Africa and Asia (Angola, Mozambique, Guinea-Bissau, Equatorial Guinea, Cape Verde, São Tomé and Príncipe, East Timor, and Macao). Moreover, Portuguese is spoken by hundreds of people right here in Connecticut and also in New Haven. In this course, we explore the varieties of Portuguese spoken around the world and how speakers who have migrated to the US have kept and/or re-constructed their identity through Portuguese and additional languages. Students also reflect on how they have become part of the Portuguese-speaking community and how Portuguese has played a role in their studies, work, personal interests, and more. This is a highly interactive and hands-on course designed to improve students' written and oral proficiency in Portuguese throughout a variety of text types (academic texts, interviews, podcasts, presentations, etc.) while fostering our sense of community. Conducted in Portuguese.
Course Title: Portuguese Around the World:  Where, How and By Whom Portuguese is Spoken

Course Description: This course examines the cinematic portrayals of military dictatorships in Brazil, Argentina, Chile, Spain, and Portugal, exploring how film serves as both a historical document and a means to reinterpret and reconstruct the past. As a language course, it allows students to engage with multiple modes of meaning–linguistic, visual, auditory, tactile, gestural, and spatial–through which cinema conveys its narratives. Students analyze how films reconstruct memory, challenge hegemonic historiography, and reinscribe erased or silenced perspectives. The course reflects on the relevance of these works in contemporary struggles against violence and oppression, considering how they teach us to critically engage with power, resistance, and collective memory. It also focuses on women's cinematic productions and representations, examining how gender, race, and political resistance intersect in the visual representation of repression, violence, and memory. The course incorporates both Spanish and Portuguese, encouraging students to express their ideas and develop projects in either language. Languages: Portuguese and Spanish.
Course Title: Through the Lens of Memory: Other Perspectives on Dictatorships in Latin America and Iberia

Course Description: Topics in health and welfare. Conversation, reading, and writing about medical issues for advanced Spanish-language students, including those considering careers in medical professions. Enrollment limited to 18.

A focused study of fiction and creative nonfiction writing. This course emphasizes the fundamentals of storytelling, narrative technique, and peer review. We examine elements such as voice, plot, conflict, character development, dialogue, and stylistic experimentation. Engaging class activities, discussions on writing technique, and analyses of contemporary works by Latinx, Latin American, and Spanish authors help you refine your creative voice, strengthen your writing skills, and deepen your understanding of the craft. Writing prompts guide exploratory exercises that support your work on longer, more polished pieces. At the end of each unit, you present your work for feedback in a workshop setting that emphasizes thoughtful dialogue and values the perspectives and experiences each writer brings. These sessions provide in-depth critique from peers and the instructor, helping you refine your drafts, strengthen your narrative style, and gain confidence in your creative process. This course is organized into two units, each centered on fiction or creative nonfiction. Your final submission is a carefully revised piece in the genre of your choice, demonstrating your command of narrative technique and your individual creative vision. This course offers an in-depth exploration of narrative genres and can be taken independently or alongside SPAN 2100. The two courses complement each other without requiring a sequence.
Course Title: Uncharted Narratives: A Creative Writing Workshop

Course Description: How do we write about literature? How do we move from reading to argument, from intuition to hypothesis, from response to analysis? Structured in three units, the writing-centered course introduces a range of critical lenses—formalist, archival, historical, feminist, ecocritical, comparative, and creative—through which the students are familiarized with different approaches to literary analysis. The main objective of the course is to develop students’ ability to formulate critical questions, construct hypotheses, and write coherent, persuasive academic arguments. To that end, the course combines theoretical reading, textual analysis of Latin American texts, and sustained writing practice. Readings include works by Jorge Luis Borges, Nicolás Guillén, Elena Garro, Clarice Lispector, João Guimarães Rosa, and Alejandra Pizarnik. The course is taught entirely in Spanish and is designed to strengthen students’ ability to engage critically with literary texts and produce clear, well-structured academic prose in Spanish.
Course Title: Writing Literature: From Reading to Argument in Latin American Texts

Course Description: Taught in Spanish, this course enhances communication skills and media literacy through the experiential analysis of art. Students engage directly with objects at the Yale Art Gallery, using curatorial study to explore how gastronomy, music, and visual arts shape history and collective memory. These experiences are complemented by riveting readings, illuminating guest speakers, and creative projects designed to benefit the community. By promoting critical citizenship, the course prepares students to debate the role of art in Latin America and Spain. Through a remote exchange with students in Peru, participants master the academic Spanish and analytical tools necessary to thrive in a globalized society.
Course Title: Language and Culture through Art: Crafting Collective Memory in the Hispanic World

Course Description: An introduction to the first literary movement of Spanish American origin, Modernismo.  At the turn of the 19th century, breaking away from Spanish Peninsular influence, modernistas looked to other languages and cultures for inspiration: from France, the U.S. and the Far East to the rich legacy of indigenous myths and traditions. Fighting for their countries' national sovereignty and for modernization, they also explored class and sexual identities and opened the way for increased participation of Spanish American women authors in literature and culture. Readings of poetry, essay, and narrative from José Martí, Manuel Gutiérrez Nájera, Rubén Darío, Delmira Agustini, Juana de Ibarborou, Lola Rodríguez de Tió, Leopoldo Lugones, Julio Herrera y Reissig, and Amado Nervo, among others. Taught in Spanish.
Course Title: Critical Contexts in Latin America: Understanding Spanish American Modernismo

Course Description: This course examines the relationship between energy systems and contemporary societies in Latin America, framed through literature, art, and environmental thought. Students will analyze the historical significance and cultural impacts of oil capitalism, nuclear energy programs, lithium extraction, and debates around renewable energy. Participants will gain insights into the legacies of colonialism, energy politics, and the environmental challenges faced by the region while exploring their artistic and cultural expressions.

This course offers an overview of the history of Latin America and the Spanish-speaking Caribbean through the lens of film. By using cinematic works as historical texts, students explore the colonial and postcolonial experiences that have shaped the region—from the era of conquest and migration to the ongoing formation of pan-ethnic Latinx identities. Through films, readings, and discussions, the course examines key themes such as colonialism and resistance, the construction of social boundaries and inequalities, and the shared yet diverse histories that connect Latin American and Caribbean societies. While this is not a film studies course, films serve as the primary tool for historical inquiry, helping students develop a critical understanding of the region’s complex past and its continued significance in global history.
Course Title: Lights, Camera, Revolution: Latin America in Film

Course Description: After English, Spanish is the most common language spoken at home in the United States. With over 41 million native speakers and 11 million foreign-language speakers, the U.S. holds the world’s second-largest Spanish-speaking population. Reflecting a history of colonialism, immigration, territorial expansion, and neocolonialism, globally, Spanish ranks second in native speakers. Unsurprisingly, Spanish-speaking authors in the U.S. now drive a dynamic Spanish-language literary production. While its roots trace back to the nineteenth century, its current shape is decisively a twenty-first-century phenomenon. Editors, writers, and scholars form a thriving community operating across prestigious creative writing programs, independent publishers, and international book fairs in cities like New York, Chicago, and Miami. In this course, we read fiction and non-fiction by acclaimed authors driving this literary movement, including Cristina Rivera Garza, Oswaldo Estrada, and Gabriela Polit Dueñas. We reflect on how these writers position themselves against U.S. histories, contexts, and social practices. Through an interdisciplinary lens combining cultural sociology, literary studies, and decolonial theory, we explore the political possibilities of this literature. We ask what writing in Spanish means in a country where the language lacks hegemony and its speakers face discrimination, supplementing our analysis with podcasts, journalism, and guest author visits.
Course Title: Uprooted Wor(l)ds: Contemporary Spanish-Language Fiction and Non-Fiction from the United States

Course Description: Changing narratives, themes, styles, and aesthetic ideals in current Brazilian prose and poetry. The writers' attempts to express or define a personal, national, and global consciousness influenced by the return of political democracy to Brazil. Focus on readings published within the last five years.

Mexico provides a revealing case through which to study how authoritarian institutions endure, electoral competition emerges, and political orders change without fully breaking from the past. This seminar traces Mexican politics from the Revolution and the construction of one-party rule to electoral competition, the rise of MORENA, and contemporary disputes over state capacity and accountability. We examine how informal practices, inequality, presidential power, and institutional weakness continue to shape political life. The course situates domestic politics within the relationship between Mexico and the United States. Migration, trade, security cooperation, organized crime, and border governance connect the two countries while generating conflicts over sovereignty and responsibility. Students learn to compare competing explanations, evaluate qualitative and quantitative evidence, interpret institutions in historical context, and distinguish scholarly arguments from political narratives. Designed as an introductory seminar, the course combines political science with history, sociology, economics, documentary film, and policy analysis. Weekly discussions, short analytical assignments, and a research project help students move from careful reading to critical argumentation.
Course Title: Mexican Politics: Evolution, Challenges, and U.S.-Mexico Relations

Course Description: Overview and analysis of politics in Latin America. The emergence of democracy and the forces that led to the unprecedented increase in inequality in the twentieth century. Topics include institutional design, historical legacies, corruption, clientelism, and violence.
Course Title: Political Power and Inequality in Latin America

Course Description: Preparation of a research paper about forty pages long under the direction of a faculty adviser, in either the fall or the spring term. Students write on subjects of their own choice. During the term before the essay is written, students plan the project in consultation with a qualified adviser or the director of undergraduate studies. The student must submit a suitable project outline and bibliography to the adviser and the director of undergraduate studies by the third week of the term. The outline should indicate the focus and scope of the essay topic, as well as the proposed research methodology. Permission may be given to write a two-term essay after consultation with an adviser and the director of undergraduate studies and after submission of a project statement. Only those who have begun to do advanced work in a given area are eligible. The requirements for the one-term senior essay apply to the two-term essay, except that the two-term essay should be substantially longer.

A project of creative work formulated and executed by the student under the supervision of a faculty adviser in the fall or spring term. Students work on projects of their own choice. Proposals for senior projects are submitted to the adviser and the director of undergraduate studies by the end of the term preceding the last resident term. An interim project review takes place by the fifth week of the term the project is developed. Permission to complete the senior project can be withdrawn if satisfactory progress has not been made. An exhibition of selected work done in the project is expected of each student.
Continuation of LATN 1001. Emphasis on consolidating grammar and on readings from Latin authors. The sequence LATN 1001 and 1002 prepares for LATN 2003.
Course Title: Beginning Latin: Review of Grammar and Selected Readings

Course Description: Continuation of LATN 1001. Emphasis on consolidating grammar and on readings from Latin authors. The sequence LATN 1001 and 1002 prepares for LATN 2003.
Course Title: Beginning Latin: Review of Grammar and Selected Readings

Course Description: Close reading of a major work of classical prose; review of grammar as needed.
An introduction to reading hexameter (epic) poetry in Latin. Readings come primarily from Vergil's Aeneid. Attention is paid both to grammar/syntax and to interpretation of poetic style and content.
An introduction to reading hexameter (epic) poetry in Latin. Readings come primarily from Vergil's Aeneid. Attention is paid both to grammar/syntax and to interpretation of poetic style and content.

Close reading of selections from Livy's Ab Urbe Condita, including Books V and XXI in Latin and additional books in English translation. The nature of representation; Augustan elements in Livy's work; themes and plots of Livian history; Livy and other Roman historians; comparison of ancient historiography and contemporary historical writing. This course is a "bridge" course, which serves as a transition from intermediate (L4) to advanced (L5) Latin.

A reading in Latin of the first book of Cicero's On the Nature of the Gods, his exposition and critique of the Epicurean theory of the gods. It is an excellent example of Cicero's philosophical method of arguing on both sides of an issue. It includes the longest connected account of Epicurean theology preserved from antiquity as well as a survey of the theology of other philosophical schools. It is an excellent example of Cicero's brilliant philosophical prose style and of his skill at characterization.
Course Title: Cicero On the Nature of the Gods I

Course Description: An in-depth study of Vergil's Aeneid within its political context.

A systematic review of syntax and an introduction to Latin style. Selections from Latin prose authors are read and analyzed, and students compose short pieces of Latin prose. For students with some experience reading Latin literature who desire a better foundation in forms, syntax, idiom, and style.

In this course, we introduce basic concepts in linguistics through the lens of rock lyrics, and discuss the ways in which this genre of language is different from (and similar to) other forms of language. Why does it sound odd to repeat the same sentence several times in a row in a conversation, but unremarkable in lyrics? Why do rock lyrics contain non-standard features of languages that their authors don't necessarily use in their their speech? Why did Sigur Rós make an entire album with speech-sounds that have no meaning? Why do so many shoegaze bands have band names that begin with sw-? What kinds of ambiguity are intentionally used to resist straightforward interpretation? Exploring these and other questions gives us a special entry point into concepts in syntax,  semantics, pragmatics, morphology, and phonology, including special topics like phonesthemes, conversational maxims, sound symbolism, and non-standard grammar, among other things.

Language as a system of mental rules, governing the sound, form, and meaning system. The (impossible) distinction between language and dialect. The scientific study of standard and non-standard varieties. Social attitudes toward prestige and other varieties; linguistic prejudice. Focus on morpho-syntactic variation in North-American English: alternative passives (“The car needs washed”), personal datives ("I need me a new printer"), negative inversion ("Don't nobody want to ride the bus"), "drama SO" ("I am SO not going to study tonight").

The study of language from the perspective of cognitive science. Exploration of mental structures that underlie the human ability to learn and process language, drawing on studies of normal and atypical language development and processing, brain imaging, neuropsychology, and computational modeling. Innate linguistic structure vs. determination by experience and culture; the relation between linguistic and nonlinguistic cognition in the domains of decision making, social cognition, and musical cognition; the degree to which language shapes perceptions of color, number, space, and gender.
Continuation of EGYP 1100.
Course Title: Introduction to Classical Hieroglyphic Egyptian II

Course Description: Continuation of SKRT 110. Focus on the basics of Sanskrit grammar; readings from classical Sanskrit texts written in Devanagari script.

An introduction to the language, literature, and culture of earliest England. A selection of both major and less-studied works of prose and verse, including charms, saints' lives, meditations on loss, a dream vision, and heroic verse, which are read in the original Old English. No prior knowledge of Old English is expected.

Introduction to language change and language history. How do people use language, and how does that lead to language change over time: sound change, analogy, syntactic and semantic change, borrowing. Techniques for recovering earlier linguistic stages: philology, internal reconstruction, the comparative method. The role of language contact in language change. Evidence from language in prehistory (doing archaeology with language); language change in individuals, and language in society

Study of formal systems that play an important role in the scientific study of language. Exploration of a range of mathematical structures and techniques; demonstrations of their application in theories of grammatical competence and performance including set theory, graphs and discrete structures, algebras, formal language, and automata theory. Evaluation of strengths and weaknesses of existing formal theories of linguistic knowledge.

Advanced work in language change focusing on practical application of methods in historical linguistics. The class gives students practice in research methods related to studying language change. Exact topics vary from year to year but could include phylogenetic analysis, methods in language and ecology, and historical reconstruction and language reclamation. An emphasis is placed on collaborative work which may result in academic publications.

Why do languages sound distinct from one another? Partly it is because different languages use different sets of sounds (in spoken languages) or signs (in signed languages) from one another. But it is also because those sounds and signs have different distributional patterns in each language. Phonology is the study of the systematic organization and patterning of sounds and signs. Students learn to describe the production of sounds and signs (articulatory phonetics), discuss restrictions on sound and sign distribution (morphemic alternation, phonotactics), and develop a model of the phonological grammar in terms of rules and representations. Throughout the course, we utilize datasets taken from a variety of the world’s languages.

A general introduction to the indigenous languages of Australia. Issues in phonology, morphology, syntax, sociolinguistics, prehistory (e.g., theories of colonization and spread), and language endangerment and revitalization.

Speakers often mean things they don’t say, but how does a hearer figure out what the speaker meant? Which sentences are designed to change the world rather than just to represent it? How are sentences used to mean different things in different contexts?  Pragmatics explores the relations between what is said and what is meant, focusing on how speech acts and the principles of “street logic”—presuppositions and implicatures—help speakers and hearers shape the landscape of a conversation.

In this course, we dive into the fascinating world of morphology, where we uncover the inner workings of words and explore how they’re constructed from smaller building blocks. As theoretical linguists—and morphologists—our objective is to understand what shapes language at the morphological level. This semester, we tackle a wide array of topics, from methods of morphological analysis to the mechanisms that seem to give language its flexibility, including affixation, reduplication, compounding, and cliticization. We also examine how morphology interacts with other areas of grammar, such as phonology and syntax.

Principles and techniques of experimental design and research in linguistics. Linguistic theory as the basis for framing experimental questions. The development of theoretically informed hypotheses, notions of control and confounds, human subject research, statistical analysis, data reporting, and dissemination.

The study of language as a cognitive neuroscience. The interaction between linguistic theory and neurological evidence from brain damage, degenerative diseases (e.g., Alzheimer's disease), mental illness (e.g., schizophrenia), neuroimaging, and neurophysiology. The connection of language as a neurocognitive system to other systems such as memory and music.

How do the cognitive processes involved in speech production relate to linguistic structure, including the morphological and phonological structure of words? This seminar engages with this question by bringing together primary readings on (1) neurocognitive models of speech motor control and (2) language-specific phonetic patterns, as they relate to morphological and phonological structure.
Course Title: Linguistic Structure in Speech Planning and Production

Course Description: Principles of phonetics, phonology, morphology, syntax, and semantics applied to the collection and interpretation of novel linguistic data. Data are collected and analyzed by the class as a group, working directly with a speaker of a relatively undocumented language. Discussion of ethics, linguistic diversity, and endangerment,

This course explores what human communication is, and how infants, children and adults take part in it. To understand this, we explore communication across the human lifespan but also across evolutionary time, looking at non-human animals or machines. Our focus is on human conversation, the development of communicative abilities that precede language, and various social dimensions of sharing information. Drawing on linguistic, philosophical, developmental and comparative research, we examine what is shared across various forms of communication, what functions it serves and where it might leave humans and human groups vulnerable.

This course continues the development of the "principles and parameters" approach to grammatical theory in Government-Binding theory and the Minimalist Program. We begin with a brief review of the architecture of syntactic theory, move on to an extended exploration of the mechanisms of dependency formation in syntax (including displacement, agreement, control, scope and anaphora), and conclude with a discussion of the nature of syntactic representation (constituency in double object constructions, the mapping between structure and thematic relations, the role of functional categories). Throughout, a major goal of the course is to engage in foundational issues by reading primary literature in syntax and applying theoretical concepts to novel data.

The model-theoretic approach to semantics and its treatment of core linguistic phenomena. Topics include quantification; tense, aspect, and modality; context and interpretation; and the semantics-pragmatics interface.

When processing language, the human mind can perform remarkable feats. For instance, we can acquire a language from a small amount of data - thousands of times less data than current systems in artificial intelligence - and we can infer what another person means even when that person’s intended message goes beyond the literal meaning of their words. This course explores how computational modeling can help us characterize our incredible capacity for language learning and processing. We focus on three modeling traditions - symbolic algorithms, Bayesian models, and neural networks - and their application to a range of psycholinguistic phenomena, including parsing, pragmatics, speech perception, word learning, and language acquisition. We also discuss how artificial intelligence can inform theories of human language processing and vice versa.

This course bridges introductory courses (LING 2630, LING 2640) and advanced seminars in semantics. It explores selected topics in some detail, allowing students to appreciate the nuances of semantic argumentation while at the same time emphasizing the foundational issues involved. The goal of this course is to allow students, within a structured format, to become comfortable engaging with open-ended problems and to gain confidence in proposing original solutions to such problems. This semester, we explore issues in formal semantics and the philosophy of language that arise in connection with the use of events. The goal is to understand the explanatory role events play in natural language semantics, the relationship between events and situations, and the interaction of events with fundamental questions in semantics, including compositionality, type theory, anaphora, negation, and semantic internalism.

Special projects set up by students with the help of a faculty adviser and the director of undergraduate studies to cover material not otherwise offered by the department. The project must terminate with at least a term paper or its equivalent and must have the approval of the director of undergraduate studies.
Research and writing of the senior essay under the guidance of a faculty adviser. Students present research related to their essays in a weekly colloquium.

This course explores applications of mathematics to politics. Students consider historical and contemporary questions about voting methods and districting through a mathematical lens, at an accessible level. These explorations engage with ideas of proof and cultivate relevant quantitative reasoning skills. Topics include ranked choice voting methods and gerrymandering.

Course Description: A continuation of MATH 1120, this course develops concepts and skills at the foundation of the STEM disciplines. In particular, we introduce Riemann sums, integration strategies, series convergence, and Taylor polynomial approximation. We use these tools to measure lengths of parametric curves, areas of polar regions and volumes of solids of revolution, and we explore applications of calculus to other disciplines including physics, economics, and statistics. MATH 1150 also focuses on strategies for problem solving, communication, and logical reasoning.

Course Description: Network structures and network dynamics described through examples and applications ranging from marketing to epidemics and the world climate. Study of social and biological networks as well as networks in the humanities. Mathematical graphs provide a simple common language to describe the variety of networks and their properties.

The course focuses on conceptual understanding and serves as an introduction to writing mathematical proofs. For an approach focused on applications rather than proofs, consider MATH 222. Students with a strong mathematical background or interest are encouraged to consider MATH 226.
